His CBC reveals a white blood cell count of 2400, hemoglobin of 7.2 g/dL her, and platelets of 32,000. Iron panel shows normal serum iron, low TIBC, but a ferritin of 7,550. Which of the following tests would help confirm the underlying diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - serum IL-2: The patient's presentation suggests a condition known as Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis (HLH). HLH is a severe hyperinflammatory syndrome that can be life-threatening if not recognized and treated promptly. Serum IL-2, or interleukin-2, is a pro-inflammatory cytokine that plays a role in the activation of immune cells. Elevated levels of IL-2, specifically the soluble IL-2 receptor (sIL-2R), are commonly seen in HLH and can serve as a diagnostic marker for the condition. This marker is often used in conjunction with other clinical and laboratory findings to help confirm the diagnosis. Incorrect Options: Option A - Serum IL-2R: While elevated soluble IL-2 receptor (sIL-2R) is commonly seen in HLH, measuring serum IL-2R directly may not be as informative as measuring the soluble form of the receptor. Option C - urine IL-10: IL-10 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine, and its elevation is not typically associated with the hyperinflammatory state seen in HLH. Option D - urine IL-10R: Similar to option c, IL-10R is not typically used as a marker for HLH diagnosis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following factors is most likely to increase the risk of development of pancreatic cancer in patients with a strong family history of pancreatic cancer in 2 first-degree relatives and a second-degree relative?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Obesity: In individuals with a hereditary risk of pancreatic cancer, other risk factors compound the possibility of disease. These include metabolic diseases like type 2 diabetes mellitus and other states of insulin resistance, as well as obesity. The primary risk factors are cigarette smoking, high body mass and lack of physical activity, pancreatic cysts, nonhereditary chronic pancreatitis, and hereditary risk factors including hereditary pancreatitis. Incorrect Options: Option A - Coffee consumption: There is conflicting evidence concerning the relationship between coffee and pancreatic cancer. Option C - NSAID use: Most studies have not found a link between aspirin and NSAID use with respect to the risk of pancreatic cancer. Option D - Diet of fruits and vegetables: A diet heavy in fruits and vegetables is inversely associated with a risk of pancreatic cancer. A high-fat diet derived primarily from meat is associated with an increased risk of pancreatic cancer. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man presents to the pulmonology clinic with a complaint of difficulty to breath and coughing. The patient has a 40-pack-year smoking history. On examination, the patient has a pink appearance and is cachectic with obvious difficulty breathing with pursed lips. The post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio is 0.6. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 75-year-old man presents to the pulmonology clinic with a complaint of difficulty to breath and coughing. The patient has a 40-pack-year smoking history. On examination, the patient has a pink appearance and is cachectic with obvious difficulty breathing with pursed lips. The post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio is 0.6. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Emphysema COPD is the persistent airflow limitation caused by obstruction of smaller airways and limitation of airflow in which FEV1/FVC < 0.70 is characteristic. Emphysema is a type of COPD characterised by the loss of alveoli due to the destruction of alveolar walls and capillaries, which result in permanent dilatation of pulmonary airspaces. These patients are cachectic with a pink appearance because the partial pressure of oxygen is not much reduced. Incorrect Options: Option A - Asthma Asthma is a chronic respiratory inflammatory disease characterised by bronchial hypersensitivity and reversible airflow obstruction. Patients present with severe shortness of breath, cough and wheezing. It may be allergic asthma due to triggers such as atopy, pollen, domestic animals, mites, mould spores and floor dust. Non-allergic asthma is due to viral respiratory tract infection, cold air, exercise-induced asthma, stress, and aspirin-induced asthma. Option C - Chronic bronchitis Chronic bronchitis is a type of COPD characterised by chronic cough with expectoration for at least three months per year for two consecutive years. A productive cough is the hallmark of the disease rather than shortness of breath. Patients are obese and have central cyanosis due to hypoxia and may also have peripheral oedema. Therefore, these patients are called “blue bloaters.” Option D - Bronchiectasis Bronchiectasis is an abnormal and irreversible dilatation of the bronchial tree due to progressive obstruction of the airway and mucous plugging by repeated bronchial inflammation. It may be caused by cystic fibrosis or after severe pneumonia, primary ciliary dyskinesia, Kartagener syndrome and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, smoking and bronchial narrowing by COPD. Patients present with copious mucopurulent sputum, repeated rhinosinusitis, and blood in sputum. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following pleural fluid results is more consistent with an exudative pleural effusion?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following pleural fluid results is more consistent with an exudative pleural effusion?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Pleural protein: Serum protein > 0.5: When differentiating between exudative and transudative effusions, Light’s criteria may be implemented, which generally consists of 3 conditions regarding protein and LDH, as follows. Pleural protein: serum protein ratio exceeds 0.5. Pleural lactate dehydrogenase (LDH): serum LDH exceeds 0.6. Pleural LDH exceeds 2/3 the upper limit of normal of LDH level. Pleural fluid analysis may be used to determine the etiology of the effusion. Transudative effusions are generally found in those with known underlying disorders such as congestive heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, or cirrhosis. In contrast, exudative effusions are more enigmatic and require further history and testing. Additional pleural fluid analysis may be obtained to help classify the exudate. Pleural pH of less than 7.3 can be associated with parapneumonic effusions, malignancy, rheumatologic effusions, or tuberculosis. Glucose of less than 50mg/dL and pH of less than 7.0 may indicate empyema needing tube thoracostomy. Incorrect Options: Option A - Pleural protein: serum protein ratio exceeds 0.5. 2. questions.stem: A 35-year-old female presents to the emergency department with complaints of severe vomiting and diarrhea for the past two days. On examination, she is dehydrated with dry mucous membranes and decreased skin turgor. Laboratory studies reveal a serum creatinine of 1.8 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen of 40 mg/dL, and a decreased urine output. Her urinalysis is unremarkable. Based on these findings, which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old female presents to the emergency department with complaints of severe vomiting and diarrhea for the past two days. On examination, she is dehydrated with dry mucous membranes and decreased skin turgor. Laboratory studies reveal a serum creatinine of 1.8 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen of 40 mg/dL, and a decreased urine output. Her urinalysis is unremarkable. Based on these findings, which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- Pre-renal acute kidney injury: In this scenario, the patient presents with dehydration, decreased urine output, an elevated BUN to creatinine ratio (>20:1), and an unremarkable urinalysis. These clinical findings suggest that pre-renal acute kidney injury (AKI) is the most likely diagnosis in this scenario. Pre-renal acute kidney injury (AKI) is a condition characterized by a sudden decrease in kidney function due to inadequate perfusion of the kidneys. Pre-renal AKI is the most common type of AKI and is often reversible with prompt recognition and treatment of the underlying cause. Pre-renal AKI can be caused by a variety of conditions that reduce blood flow to the kidneys, including: Dehydration due to vomiting, diarrhea, or excessive sweating. Hypotension due to sepsis, anaphylaxis, or heart failure. Reduced cardiac output, such as in myocardial infarction or arrhythmias Obstruction of the renal artery or vein Medications such as non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors Symptoms of pre-renal AKI include decreased urine output, dry mouth, decreased skin turgor, and dizziness. Laboratory tests reveal elevated creatinine and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) levels. BUN to creatinine ratio is used to help differentiate pre-renal AKI from other types of AKI. In pre-renal AKI, the ratio is typically greater than 20:1, while in other types of AKI, the ratio is often lower. Other investigations include the fractional excretion of sodium (< 1% in pre-renal AKI) and urine Na (< 20 mmol/L). Urinalysis is often normal. The treatment of pre-renal AKI involves identifying and treating the underlying cause. This may include rehydration with intravenous fluids, treatment of hypotension, correction of electrolyte imbalances, or removal of any offending medications. In severe cases, renal replacement therapy (dialysis) may be necessary. Incorrect Options: Option A- Acute tubular necrosis: Acute tubular necrosis (ATN) is a type of AKI that occurs due to damage to the renal tubules within the kidney, often due to ischemia or nephrotoxic medications. However, urinalysis shows granular casts. Therefore, ATN is less likely to be the cause of the AKI as this patient has a normal urinalysis. Option B- Glomerulonephritis: Glomerulonephritis is a type of kidney inflammation that can cause AKI. However, urinalysis shows the presence of blood and protein, which is not present in this scenario. Therefore, glomerulonephritis is less likely to be the cause of AKI. Option C- Interstitial nephritis: Interstitial nephritis is another type of kidney inflammation that can cause AKI. However, this condition is usually associated with eosinophils in the urine and systemic symptoms such as fever and rash, which are not mentioned in this scenario. Therefore, interstitial nephritis is less likely to be the cause of AKI. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with a history of substance use disorder is transported to the emergency department by his wife. Upon arrival, he is somnolent and difficult to arouse. His blood pressure is 100/80 mmHg, respiratory rate is 11 breaths/minute, and heart rate is 60 beats/minute. Pupils are constricted and bowel sounds are decreased. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial medication to administer?
questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old man with a history of substance use disorder is transported to the emergency department by his wife. Upon arrival, he is somnolent and difficult to arouse. His blood pressure is 100/80 mmHg, respiratory rate is 11 breaths/minute, and heart rate is 60 beats/minute. Pupils are constricted and bowel sounds are decreased. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial medication to administer?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- Naloxone: This patient is suffering from opioid intoxication , as indicated by his clinical presentation. Signs of opioid intoxication include depressed mental status, miosis, decreased respiratory rate and tidal volume; decreased bowel sounds, nausea, vomiting, and severe itching . The patient's heart rate can be normal to low. Hypotension may occur as a result of histamine release, but it is not consistently seen. Overdose that involves opioid drugs is a life-threatening situation. Fatal respiratory depression can occur due to direct suppression of respiratory centers in the midbrain and medulla. Naloxone is a strong antagonist of µ-opioid receptors , a medium antagonist of kappa-opioid receptors, and a weak antagonist of delta-opioid receptors. Opioid intoxication is treated with naloxone, adequate hydration, mechanical ventilation. Incorrect Options: Option A- Acamprosate: Acamprosate is an anti-craving drug used for maintenance therapy of alcohol withdrawal. Option B- Bupropion: Bupropion is used for nicotine withdrawal and acts on dopamine and noradrenaline receptors. MR angiography demonstrated an ascending aorta intimal flap confirming the type B aortic dissection diagnosis. Which of the following represents the next step in this patient's management?
questions.solution: Correct Option A- Medical management: Type B aortic dissection involves only descending aorta. Stanford Type B aortic dissection is handled medically. The major goal of medical care is to maintain mean arterial pressure between 60 and 75 mmHg to lessen the left ventricle's ejection force. Beta-blockers, notably labetalol, which also has alpha-blocking effects, are the first line of treatment. When beta blockers are contraindicated , rate-controlling calcium channel blockers like diltiazem or verapamil are employed. Sodium nitroprusside is used when both beta blockers and calcium channel blockers fail to reduce blood pressure. Incorrect Options: Option B- Surgery: Surgery is the best course of action for patients with type A aortic dissection. The ascending aorta is replaced during emergency surgery for Type A dissection. The morbidity and mortality of surgery are quite high, and type B aneurysms are surgically treated when there is a real risk of exterior rupture and risk of limb or important organ (kidneys, gut) ischemia. Option C- Surveillance by USG: Regular surveillance with USG has been suggested in patients with an asymptomatic aortic aneurysm whose size is less than 5.5cm. There is no role of surveillance with USG in patients with aortic dissection. Option D- No treatment: Treatment is urgently needed since acute dissection has an early death rate of 1-5% each hour. Patients with aortic dissection need emergency treatment. @Neet_pg_bot

A chest radiograph reveals consolidation in the right lower lobe. Which of the following treatments should the patient receive?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Supportive care only: This patient most likely has aspiration pneumonitis , which is an inflammatory chemical injury to the lower airway due to the inhalation of acidic stomach contents. Aspiration pneumonia may occur later when the lungs’ defenses are damaged by chemical irritation. This is one of the leading causes of community acquired pneumonia, as 50% of normal adults and 70% of the elderly aspirate while they sleep. Aspiration of gastric contents with a pH <2.5 and at least 0.3 mL/kg of volume is required to cause pneumonitis. The caustic effect of the aspirated fluid occurs quickly, and is manifested with cough, chest pain, shortness of breath, and fevers. The most common chest X-ray finding in affected individuals is a right lower lobe consolidation, but bilateral or interstitial patterns are also seen. Patients with aspiration pneumonitis should be managed supportively . Suctioning and/or endotracheal intubation for airway protection should be done if deemed clinically necessary. Bronchodilators may help with aspiration-induced bronchospasm. Incorrect Options: Option B - Clindamycin and parenteral steroids: There is no evidence that prophylactic antibiotics or steroids provide any benefit to patients. Option C - Clindamycin only: However, there is consensus that patients with symptoms of pneumonitis for more than 24-48 hours should begin receiving antibiotics. Option D - Parenteral steroids only: Suctioning and/or endotracheal intubation for airway protection should be done if deemed clinically necessary. Bronchodilators may help with aspiration-induced bronchospasm. @Neet_pg_bot

He also noticed that his urine appeared darker than usual, and for the last 2 days, he has passed only small amounts of urine. His temperature is 37.5°C (98.6°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 15/min, and blood pressure is 154/98 mm Hg. Examination shows 2+ pretibial oedema bilaterally. The renal biopsy specimen shows a crescent formation in the glomeruli with extra capillary cell proliferation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- Administer Methylprednisolone: Patients with RPGN should start receiving intravenous glucocorticoids right away to suppress their immune systems. Additionally, since it significantly lowers the risk of recurrence, combination therapy with cyclophosphamide is typically advised. After that, blood pressure management should start. In addition, careful monitoring of kidney function is necessary to determine whether renal replacement therapy (RRT) is necessary. A high risk of death and progression to end-stage renal disease exists in the absence of appropriate treatment. Incorrect Options: Option A- Administer Lisinopril: ACE inhibitors such as lisinopril are first-line drugs in the management of hypertension and are particularly beneficial for patients with kidney disease and proteinuria due to their nephroprotective properties. Although strict blood pressure control is certainly indicated for future management of this patient's hypertension, administering lisinopril is not the most appropriate next step in the definitive management of RPGN. Option B- Perform Hemodialysis: Hemodialysis is the most common form of renal replacement therapy used in the US. Although dialysis may be required to manage renal failure in patients with RPGN, this patient does not present with findings that would warrant dialysis. Supportive management with sufficient hydration, antihypertensive drugs, and diuretics should be initiated. More importantly, this patient requires immediate immunomodulatory therapy to manage the underlying cause of RPGN. Option C- Perform Plasmapheresis: Plasmapheresis is performed in patients with RPGN due to Goodpasture syndrome to eliminate anti-GBM antibodies. However, patients with RPGN are at significant risk of developing end-stage renal failure. Preparation for plasmapheresis should not delay medical treatment. Furthermore, Goodpasture syndrome is a pulmonary-renal syndrome, which typically manifests with the nephritic syndrome as well as the pulmonary symptom. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old patient presents with a fever and an ulcerative lesion at the site of a tick bite on the upper extremity. Tender lymphadenopathy of the axilla is noted. Serologic testing confirms a diagnosis of tularemia. Treatment with tetracycline is initiated. Which of the following is the correct mechanism of action for this treatment?

options.label: A
options.text: Inactivation of enzymes in the bacterial cell membrane

options.label: B
options.text: Reversible binding to the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit

options.label: C
options.text: Inhibition of enzymes involved in tetrahydrofolic acid synthesis

options.label: D
options.text: Binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit and inhibiting protein synthesis

questions.answerText: Reversible binding to the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Reversible binding to the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit is the MOA of doxycycline: Doxycycline is a tetracycline antibiotic. The mechanism of action is through reversible binding to the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit, leading eventually to inhibition of bacterial protein synthesis. The tetracyclines are broad-spectrum bacteriostatic antibiotics used to treat many aerobic gram-positive and gram-negative infections. They are also active against atypical bacteria such as Rickettsia species. The most common side effects involve the gastrointestinal system. In general, tetracyclines should not be used in pregnant women (unless other medications are not effective or contraindicated) due to possible fetal toxicity, or in young children under 8 years of age due to the potential for tooth discoloration. Incorrect Options: Option A - Inactivation of enzymes in the bacterial cell membrane: Beta-lactam antibiotics such as penicillin inhibit bacterial growth by inactivating enzymes located in the bacterial cell wall. Option C - Inhibition of enzymes involved in tetrahydrofolic acid synthesis: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole works by inhibiting enzymes involved in the synthesis of tetrahydrofolic acid, which subsequently inhibits DNA synthesis. Option D - Binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit and inhibiting protein synthesis: Macrolides (e.g. azithromycin, erythromycin) inhibit bacterial protein synthesis by binding the bacterial 50S subunit. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man with a history of asthma since childhood presents to the emergency room with respiratory distress and wheezing. He has had numerous asthma exacerbations in the recent past requiring intubation. On physical examination, he has a temperature of 36.9°C, blood pressure of 142/85 mmHg, heart rate of 124/minute, respiratory rate of 26/minute, and oxygen saturation of 94% while on 2L/min nasal cannula. He is visibly dyspneic and unable to complete full sentences. Significant supraclavicular retractions, bilateral wheezing, and a prolonged expiratory phase are noted. Cardiac exam is unremarkable except for tachycardia. Abdomen is soft and non-tender. He has no lower extremity edema. What hemodynamic changes occur during inspiration compared to expiration in this patient?
questions.stemHtml:
A 22-year-old man with a history of asthma since childhood presents to the emergency room with respiratory distress and wheezing. He has had numerous asthma exacerbations in the recent past requiring intubation. On physical examination, he has a temperature of 36.9°C, blood pressure of 142/85 mmHg, heart rate of 124/minute, respiratory rate of 26/minute, and oxygen saturation of 94% while on 2L/min nasal cannula. He is visibly dyspneic and unable to complete full sentences. Significant supraclavicular retractions, bilateral wheezing, and a prolonged expiratory phase are noted.
Cardiac exam is unremarkable except for tachycardia. Abdomen is soft and non-tender. He has no lower extremity edema. What hemodynamic changes occur during inspiration compared to expiration in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased right ventricular preload, increased pulmonary capacitance, increased left ventricular preload, increased left ventricular afterload

options.label: B
options.text: Increased right ventricular preload, increased pulmonary capacitance, decreased left ventricular preload, increased left ventricular afterload

options.label: C
options.text: Decreased right ventricular preload, decreased pulmonary capacitance, increased left ventricular preload, decreased left ventricular afterload

questions.answerText: Increased right ventricular preload, increased pulmonary capacitance, decreased left ventricular preload, increased left ventricular afterload
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Increased right ventricular preload, increased pulmonary capacitance, decreased left ventricular preload, increased left ventricular afterload: The patient is in the midst of an asthma exacerbation. Because of increased airways resistance, he is requiring much wider swings in pleural pressure to get air in and out of his lungs, as manifested by his supraclavicular retractions. These intensified swings in pleural pressure result in hemodynamic changes that ultimately lead to pulsus paradoxus, a condition with significant variation in systolic blood pressure in relation to the respiratory cycle. During inspiration, pleural pressure is negative, which results in negative intrathoracic pressure. Negative intrathoracic pressure decreases the right atrial pressure, resulting in increased venous return to the right side of the heart and increased right ventricular preload. With more negative intrathoracic pressure, there is less “squeezing” of the pulmonary vasculature and more blood can remain in the pulmonary vasculature, resulting in an increase in pulmonary capacitance. Increased abdominal pressure also raises the gradient for systemic venous return. The net effect of increased abdominal pressure in the presence of normo‐ or hypervolemia is an increased systemic venous return. Because of increased right ventricular preload, the right ventricular size will increase, causing a bulge of the intraventricular septum into the left ventricle, reducing the ability of the left ventricle to fill properly, resulting in a decrease in left ventricular preload. Left ventricular preload is also reduced because more blood is staying in the pulmonary vasculature instead of entering the left side of the heart in increased pulmonary capacitance. Left ventricular afterload is defined as the amount of work that the left ventricle has to do to eject blood. If intrathoracic pressure is decreased, there is less assistance from the pressure outside of the left ventricle to squeeze the left heart to eject blood; therefore, the left ventricle has to work harder by increasing wall stress to eject blood, which increasing left ventricular afterload. Note that positive intrathoracic pressure actually reduces left ventricular afterload, and positive intrathoracic pressure “squeezes” the left ventricle, assisting it to eject blood and reducing the amount of work it has to do. Incorrect Options: Option A - Increased right ventricular preload, increased pulmonary capacitance, increased left ventricular preload, increased left ventricular afterload: During an asthma exacerbation, left ventricular preload actually decreases. This is due to the increased pulmonary capacitance (more blood remaining in the pulmonary vasculature) and because of the septal shift caused by increased right ventricular preload. The septal shift reduces the ability of the left ventricle to fill properly, leading to decreased left ventricular preload. Option C - Decreased right ventricular preload, decreased pulmonary capacitance, increased left ventricular preload, decreased left ventricular afterload: Right ventricular preload and pulmonary capacitance increase, not decrease, during an asthma exacerbation due to negative intrathoracic pressure, which results from the increased effort to inhale against constricted airways. This leads to a greater volume of blood returning to the right side of the heart (increased right ventricular preload) and more blood remaining in the pulmonary vasculature (increased pulmonary capacitance). Additionally, left ventricular afterload increases, not decreases, during inspiration because the heart has to work harder to eject blood when intrathoracic pressure decreases. Option D - Increased right ventricular preload, increased pulmonary capacitance, decreased left ventricular preload, decreased left ventricular afterload: Although it correctly identifies the changes in preload and pulmonary capacitance, it incorrectly suggests that left ventricular afterload decreases. As mentioned, during inspiration, left ventricular afterload actually increases. The heart has to work harder to eject blood due to the decreased intrathoracic pressure, thereby increasing left ventricular afterload. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 42 year old female patient who completed a MUD transplant for Ph+ ALL follows up with you on day 120 of her transplant. Her course was complicated by acute GVHD of the liver and was treated with steroids and ruxolitnib. She has been tapered off successfully but is still on 5mg per day of steroids. Which of the following is not a risk factor for the development of chronic graft versus host disease in a stem cell transplant recipient?
questions.stemHtml: A 42 year old female patient who completed a MUD transplant for Ph+ ALL follows up with you on day 120 of her transplant. Her course was complicated by acute GVHD of the liver and was treated with steroids and ruxolitnib. She has been tapered off successfully but is still on 5mg per day of steroids. Which of the following is not a risk factor for the development of chronic graft versus host disease in a stem cell transplant recipient?

options.label: D
options.text: Peripheral blood stem cell rather than bone marrow or umbilical cord

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Male donor for female recipient: Chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD) is a complex and multifactorial condition that can develop after allogeneic stem cell transplantation. questions.stemHtml: Which of the following prescription medications is most commonly cited as a cause of methemoglobinemia?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Dapsone: Dapsone is commonly cited as a prescription medication that can cause methemoglobinemia, a condition where the iron in hemoglobin is converted from its ferrous (Fe2+) state to the ferric (Fe3+) state. This conversion impairs the ability of hemoglobin to effectively bind and release oxygen, leading to decreased oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood. Methemoglobinemia can result in a bluish or cyanotic appearance of the skin and mucous membranes (cyanosis), as well as symptoms of oxygen deprivation such as shortness of breath, confusion, and lethargy. In severe cases, it can lead to respiratory distress and even death if left untreated. Dapsone is an antibiotic used to treat conditions such as dermatitis herpetiformis and pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) prophylaxis in certain populations. It's known to cause methemoglobinemia by oxidizing hemoglobin, resulting in the formation of methemoglobin. Incorrect Options: Option B - Aspirin: While aspirin can cause a range of adverse effects, including gastrointestinal bleeding and Reye's syndrome, it is not commonly associated with methemoglobinemia. Option C - Chloroquine: Chloroquine is an antimalarial medication. While it can have side effects, methemoglobinemia is not a well-established side effect of chloroquine. Option D - Nitroglycerine: Nitroglycerine is a medication used for the treatment of angina and other cardiovascular conditions. It primarily works as a vasodilator and is not typically associated with causing methemoglobinemia. @Neet_pg_bot

Crepitus can be found sometimes when there is a large subsequent pneumomediastinum. Incorrect Options: Option A- Uncontrolled hypertension: Although hypertension is a common complication of end-stage renal disease, it does not indicate renal transplantation. Hypertension can usually be managed with medications and lifestyle changes, and kidney transplantation may not necessarily improve hypertension control. Transplantation may improve glucose control in some patients, but other treatments can also achieve glycemic control . Option D- Polycystic kidney disease: Polycystic kidney disease (PKD) is a genetic disorder that causes cysts to form in the kidneys, leading to progressive kidney damage and end-stage renal disease. questions.solution: Correct Option A – 5: Traditionally, an uncuffed endotracheal tube has been preferred in children younger than 8 years old , and the rule of thumb to determine size is generally ( Age/4) + 4. The cricoid ring may form a physiologic cuff on the tube. There is, however, evidence that cuffed tubes may be safely used in paediatric patients of all ages and may provide greater airway protection. For an uncuffed ET tube in paediatric patients, the formula used is (Age/4) + 4. This mutation results in the failure of B cell maturation and subsequent absence or reduction in immunoglobulins (antibodies), particularly IgM and IgG. Patients with XLA have a characteristic clinical presentation with recurrent pyogenic infections, including pneumonia and otitis media, due to the absence of functional B cells and the resulting inability to produce effective antibody responses. Hypoplasia of lymphoid tissue is also a common finding due to the absence of mature B cells. Incorrect Options: Option A - Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID): CVID is a primary immunodeficiency disorder characterized by decreased levels of immunoglobulins (antibodies) in the blood and a variable age of onset. Option C - Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID): SCID is a severe primary immunodeficiency disorder characterized by a profound deficiency in both B and T cell function. It usually presents early in life and is associated with severe and recurrent infections. SCID is not likely in this case, as the patient's T cell count is reported as normal, whereas in SCID, both B and T cells are severely affected. questions.solution: Correct Option D - Daily low dose aspirin and hydroxyurea: The vignette describes a diagnosis of essential thrombocythemia (ET) with an identified mutation in the MPL gene which encodes the thrombopoietin receptor. This patient would have intermediate risk ET given age > 60, MPL mutation, and no personal history of thrombosis. It is reasonable to consider for these patients low dose aspirin and cytoreductive therapy typically with hydroxyurea to reduce the long term thrombotic risk to the patient. Incorrect Options: Option A - Romiplostim: Romiplostim is a thrombopoietin receptor agonist that can be used to treat thrombocytopenia (low platelet count), particularly in conditions like immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). However, in the case described, the patient has thrombocytosis (elevated platelet count), which is a hallmark of ET. Using romiplostim to further increase platelet count is not appropriate and may exacerbate the condition. However, it is not typically used as a first-line therapy for ET, especially in asymptomatic patients without significant disease-related complications. questions.stem: A 28-year-old female came to the clinic complaining that she had not been menstruating for the last 4 months. She has previously normal menses every 28 days that last for 3 to 4 days. Her urine pregnancy test is negative. Laboratory evaluation reveals normal thyroid hormone levels; however, prolactin levels are 300 ng/mL, and prolactinoma was suspected. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic modality for this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old female came to the clinic complaining that she had not been menstruating for the last 4 months. She has previously normal menses every 28 days that last for 3 to 4 days. Her urine pregnancy test is negative. Laboratory evaluation reveals normal thyroid hormone levels; however, prolactin levels are 300 ng/mL, and prolactinoma was suspected. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic modality for this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - MRI with contrast: This patient is suspected of having prolactinoma given her history of secondary amenorrhea, negative pregnancy test, and elevated prolactin levels (> 200 ng/mL). Prolactin-secreting tumours of the pituitary gland are called prolactinomas. It is the most common secretory tumour of the pituitary gland. Prolactinomas arise from the monoclonal expansion of pituitary lactotrophs that have undergone somatic mutation. Based on the size of the tumours, prolactinomas can be classified as micro prolactinoma (smaller than 10 mm), macroprolactinoma (larger than 10 mm), or giant prolactinoma (larger than 4 cm) Prolactin levels are usually directly proportionate to the size of the tumour, ranging from below 200 ng/ml with less than 1 cm, 200 ng/ml to 1000 ng/ml with 1 cm to 2 cm, and more than 1000 ng/ml with tumour size more than 2 cm in diameter. A detailed history and physical examination are required to rule out the reversible causes of hyperprolactinemia, i.e. pregnancy, hypothyroidism, and medications. MRI with gadolinium is the preferred imaging modality for evaluating hyperprolactinemia as it best describes the anatomy of the hypothalamic-pituitary area. Incorrect Options: Option A - CT scan with contrast: It is not the most appropriate test to visualize the pituitary adenoma as the anatomy of the hypothalamic-pituitary area is not visible. Option B - Biopsy of the adenoma: It is not used for diagnosing prolactinoma because it is an invasive procedure with no added advantage over other tests. Option C - MR venography: MR venography is used to diagnose the conditions involving the cerebral veins, i.e. idiopathic intracranial hypertension and cerebral venous thrombosis secondary to a hypercoagulable state. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man arrives at the emergency department reporting palpitations, chest discomfort, and lightheadedness. An electrocardiogram (ECG) reveals regular tachycardia with normal QRS complexes. Based on these findings, what is the most probable diagnosis for this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 30-year-old man arrives at the emergency department reporting palpitations, chest discomfort, and lightheadedness. An electrocardiogram (ECG) reveals regular tachycardia with normal QRS complexes. Based on these findings, what is the most probable diagnosis for this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Atrioventricular nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT): The patient's symptoms and ECG findings are consistent with the diagnosis of supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), specifically AVNRT. AVNRT is a regular tachycardia with normal QRS complexes caused by a re-entry circuit involving the AV node and its right atrial input pathways. Symptoms include chest discomfort, palpitations, lightheadedness, or breathlessness. Management options include carotid sinus pressure or the Valsalva manoeuvre for acute episodes, while adenosine, verapamil, intravenous β-blockers, or flecainide can restore sinus rhythm in most cases. DC cardioversion may be necessary for severe hemodynamic compromise. Catheter ablation is the most effective therapy for recurrent SVT, with a success rate of over 90%. Prophylaxis with oral β-blockers, verapamil, or flecainide may also be used, but long-term drug therapy can create difficulties in female patients during pregnancy. Incorrect Options: Option A- Ventricular tachycardia: Ventricular tachycardia (VT) is a rapid heart rhythm originating in the ventricles , the heart's lower chambers. VT is typically defined as a run of three or more consecutive ventricular beats at a rate of 100 beats per minute or faster. The condition can be sustained or non-sustained, meaning it can last for a short or extended period. VT can occur in patients with structural heart disease, such as previous heart attacks, cardiomyopathy, or valvular heart disease , and in patients with a normal heart. Some patients may experience symptoms such as palpitations, chest discomfort, shortness of breath, or dizziness, while others may be asymptomatic. VT can be diagnosed with an electrocardiogram (ECG) and confirmed with further testing, such as a Holter monitor or electrophysiology study. The treatment of VT depends on the underlying cause and the patient's symptoms. It may involve medication, cardioversion, ablation , or an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD). VT can be a life-threatening arrhythmia , and prompt treatment is essential to prevent complications such as cardiac arrest, heart failure, or sudden death. Option B- Atrial fibrillation: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a common cardiac arrhythmia associated with risk factors such as hypertension, heart failure, and structural heart disease. Diagnosis is confirmed on ECG, which shows an irregularly irregular rhythm with no discernible P waves. AF can be classified as paroxysmal, persistent, or permanent. Management includes rate control, rhythm control, and anticoagulation therapy based on the patient's symptoms, comorbidities, and risk of thromboembolism. Complications of AF include stroke, heart failure, and increased mortality, highlighting the importance of early detection and optimal management. Option D- Atrial flutter: Atrial flutter is an abnormal heart rhythm in the heart's upper chambers (atria). It creates a circular movement in the right atrium, seen as a saw-tooth pattern on ECG. Heart rate is usually around 150 bpm but can be as high as 300 bpm. Atrial flutter can cause a 2:1, 3:1, or 4:1 block of impulses to the lower chambers (ventricles), leading to a slower heart rate. Symptoms include palpitations, shortness of breath, and fatigue. Medical treatment includes digoxin, beta-blockers, or verapamil to control heart rate. Direct current cardioversion can restore normal rhythm; catheter ablation may be recommended. Anticoagulation therapy may be necessary to prevent blood clots. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 35 year-old female was a restrained passenger in a rollover motor vehicle collision in which the driver was fatally injured. She requires intubation and mechanical ventilation, with assist control at a tidal volume of 400 mL (plateau pressure of 28), respiratory rate of 14 breaths per minute, positive end expiratory pressure (PEEP) of 5, and supplementary oxygen at a concentration of 60%. An arterial blood gas sample obtained 15 minutes after intubation reveals a pH of 7.2, PaCO2 of 48 mm Hg, PaO2 of 98 mm Hg and HCO3 of 23 mEq/L. Which of the following changes to the ventilator would most likely benefit this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 35 year-old female was a restrained passenger in a rollover motor vehicle collision in which the driver was fatally injured. She requires intubation and mechanical ventilation, with assist control at a tidal volume of 400 mL (plateau pressure of 28), respiratory rate of 14 breaths per minute, positive end expiratory pressure (PEEP) of 5, and supplementary oxygen at a concentration of 60%. An arterial blood gas sample obtained 15 minutes after intubation reveals a pH of 7.2, PaCO2 of 48 mm Hg, PaO2 of 98 mm Hg and HCO3 of 23 mEq/L. Which of the following changes to the ventilator would most likely benefit this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Increase the respiratory rate: The patient's arterial blood gases in this setting suggest acute respiratory acidosis . To correct this patient's acidosis, ventilation should be increased to eliminate CO2. Ventilation is a function of respiratory rate and the tidal volume minus dead space. Increasing the tidal volume will improve CO2 elimination to correct the acidosis, but increased tidal volumes are associated with an increased plateau pressure. Plateau pressure is the static pressure in the lung at the end of inspiration. It reflects both lung compliance and alveolar pressure. When utilizing a lung protective ventilation strategy based on the ARDSNet data, plateau pressures should remain below 30mm H20 to prevent damage to the lower airway. Higher pressures are associated with increased risk of barotrauma, particularly in conditions in which lung compliance is reduced, such as ARDS. An increase in the respiratory rate will provide an increase in minute ventilation, which will increase elimination of CO2 and correct acidosis without the risk of barotrauma that is associated with large tidal volumes. Two strategies to improve ventilation are increase in the respiratory rate and increase in tidal volume. Oxygenation can be improved by increased FiO2 and/or increased mean alveolar pressure, which is achieved by increased PEEP or by an increase in the I:E ratio. Incorrect Options: Option A - Increase the tidal volume: Increasing the tidal volume is more likely to result in barotrauma compared to use of increased respiratory rate to increase the patient's minute ventilation. Option B - Increase the PEEP: Increasing the PEEP will improve oxygenation, but it does not improve elimination of CO2 and will not change the patient's pH. The patient is not hypoxic, so increased PEEP is not indicated. questions.answerText: Identify the presence of P waves and assess their regularity with the QRS complexes.
questions.solution: Correct Option B- Identify the presence of P waves and assess their regularity to the QRS complexes:: P waves must be found and their regularity in relation to the QRS complexes must be evaluated to determine rhythm on an ECG. Atrial depolarization is indicated by the presence of a P wave, whereas ventricular depolarization is shown by the QRS complex. The rhythm is regarded as sinus if both the P waves and the QRS complexes are regular. Incorrect Options: Option A- Count the number of QRS complexes in a 6-second interval and multiply by 10 to get the beats per minute: The above-mentioned method is used to calculate heart rate and not rhythm. But, this method is only used for heart calculation if there are no abnormal beats. So, this option is incorrect Option C- Look at the shape and duration of the T waves and assess their regularity in relation to the QRS complexes: P waves should be followed by QRS in normal rhythm electrocardiograms. This shows that the rhythm is regular, and the relation between T wave and QRS complex. Option D- Measure the distance between R waves: Measuring the distance between two R waves will give the heart rate if 60 is divided by it. This is known as the R-R interval @Neet_pg_bot

Incorrect Options:

Option C- Look at the shape and duration of the T waves and assess their regularity in relation to the QRS complexes:

  • P waves should be followed by QRS in normal rhythm electrocardiograms.

  • Measuring the distance between two R waves will give the heart rate if 60 is divided by it.

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Orthostatic tremor Orthostatic tremor is a rare disorder characterized by leg tremor upon standing. Fear of falling and unsteadiness are common. Symptoms usually start in the sixth decade of life. Tremor resolves when the patient starts walking, sits down, or leans against a wall or counter. Diagnosis is confirmed by surface electromyogram demonstrating a synchronous 13-18 Hz tremor of the legs. Auscultation of the legs with a stethoscope may also reveal a thumping sound. Orthostatic tremor is usually idiopathic but may be seen in association with other movement disorders. Incorrect Options: Option A. -Progressive Supranuclear Palsy (PSP): PSP is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by supranuclear gaze palsy, postural instability, parkinsonism, and cognitive changes. It doesn't typically present with isolated leg tremor that is only present upon standing. Option B - Idiopathic Parkinson's Disease: While Parkinson's disease can cause resting tremors, it is unlikely to present with a tremor that is limited to the legs and only occurs upon standing. Parkinson's tremors tend to be present at rest and can also occur during movement. Option D - Task-Specific Dystonia: Task-specific dystonia involves involuntary muscle contractions during specific actions, such as writing or playing a musical instrument. It does not typically manifest as a tremor that is limited to standing and stops during walking. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male textile worker for the past twenty years presents to the clinic with a productive cough for the last two months. Physical examination reveals wheezing and decreased breath sounds in the lungs. Chest x-ray shows haziness in the lower lobes of the lungs. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old male textile worker for the past twenty years presents to the clinic with a productive cough for the last two months. Physical examination reveals wheezing and decreased breath sounds in the lungs. Chest x-ray shows haziness in the lower lobes of the lungs. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Byssinosis: Byssinosis is an occupational lung disease caused by exposure to cotton, flax, and hemp dust. Workers in industries such as cotton mills and textile factories plants are at risk of developing byssinosis. Clinical features of acute byssinosis include the following: Acute byssinosis occurs after short-term exposure to cotton dust and is usually reversible. The symptoms of acute byssinosis typically appear within hours of exposure to cotton dust. Symptoms include cough, wheezing, shortness of breath, chest tightness, and fever. These symptoms typically worsen on the first day of work after a period of time off, such as on a Monday after a weekend break, and improve as the week progresses. Clinical features of chronic byssinosis include the following: Long-term exposure to cotton dust leads to chronic byssinosis. The cyclical features of acute byssinosis disappear, and the patient presents with a chronic productive cough. Diagnosis of byssinosis involves: Pulmonary function tests: Decreased FEV1 and normal or increased FEV1/FVC. Chest x-ray: Haziness in the lower lobes of the lungs. Management of byssinosis includes: Avoid exposure to cotton dust Inhaled corticosteroids Bronchodilators Oral corticosteroids are reserved for severe cases Incorrect Options: Option B - Asbestosis: Asbestosis is an interstitial lung disease caused by the inhalation of asbestos fibers. Individuals working in shipbuilding, insulation, roofing, mining, and firefighting equipment manufacturing industries are at risk of inhaling asbestos fibres. Chest x-ray shows pleural plaques and parenchymal infiltrates in the lower lobes of the lung. The textile industry does not expose the individual to asbestos; hence, this diagnosis of asbestosis is less likely. Option C - Silicosis: The inhalation of silica dust in mining, sandblasting, and construction industries is responsible for causing silicosis. Eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes and small nodules in the upper lobes of the lung are seen on chest x-ray. This patient is unlikely to be exposed to silica dust while working in the textile industry. Option D - Pneumoconiosis: Exposure to coal dust can cause coal worker’s pneumoconiosis (CWP). CWP is characterised by the accumulation of coal dust particles in the lungs, which can lead to inflammation and fibrosis. Chest x-rays may show small nodules in the upper lobes of the lung. This patient’s occupation and haziness in the lower lobes make the diagnosis of pneumoconiosis less likely. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Left-beating nystagmus in primary gaze, abnormal head-impulse testing when thrusting to the right, increase in nystagmus when gazing to the left, with no vertical ocular misalignment The HINTS test (Head Impulse – Nystagmus – Test of Skew) is a 3-step bedside oculomotor examination maneuver designed to have maximal sensitivity for the clinical diagnosis of acute stroke in patients presenting with an acute vestibular syndrome, even in cases where the initial diffusion-weighted MRI imaging is negative. In a pivotal study from 2009, 100% of patients with acute stroke were accurately detected with 96% specificity when any 1 of the 3 were found: normal head impulse testing, direction-changing nystagmus, or skew deviation. Option B is the only one that lists a set of findings that do not violate one of these 3 rules. Incorrect Options: Option A - Left-Beating Nystagmus in Primary Gaze, Normal Head-Impulse Testing When Thrusting to the Right, Increase in Nystagmus When Gazing to the Left, With No Vertical Ocular Misalignment The presence of left-beating nystagmus in primary gaze and an increase in nystagmus when gazing to the left could be indicative of vestibular dysfunction or peripheral vertigo. However, normal head-impulse testing suggests intact peripheral vestibular function, which may not be consistent with the diagnosis of acute vestibular neuritis. Acute vestibular neuritis often results in reduced or absent responses during head-impulse testing on the affected side due to impaired function of the vestibular nerve. Option C - Right-Beating Nystagmus in Primary Gaze, Normal Head-Impulse Testing When Thrusting to the Left, Left-Beating Nystagmus When Gazing to the Left, With No Vertical Ocular Misalignment The combination of right-beating nystagmus in primary gaze and left-beating nystagmus when gazing to the left is not characteristic of a typical vestibular disorder. The normal head-impulse testing when thrusting to the left also suggests intact peripheral vestibular function. Option D - Right-Beating Nystagmus in Primary Gaze, Abnormal Head-Impulse Testing When Thrusting to the Left, Increase in Nystagmus When Gazing to the Right, With a Noticeable Vertical Ocular Misalignment While right-beating nystagmus and abnormal head-impulse testing suggest a peripheral vestibular disorder, the noticeable vertical ocular misalignment is not typical of peripheral vertigo. Vertical ocular misalignment could be associated with central nervous system (CNS) pathology rather than peripheral vestibular dysfunction. @Neet_pg_bot

options.label: A
options.text: If the mother has active drug-susceptible pulmonary TB and the infant has no evidence of active or latent TB, both the mother and infant should be treated for active TB.

options.label: B
options.text: Exclusively breastfed infants receiving isoniazid via breast milk should receive supplemental pyridoxine.

options.label: C
options.text: If both the mother and infant have active pulmonary TB, they should be separated until the completion of 2 weeks of treatment.

options.label: D

questions.answerText: Exclusively breastfed infants receiving isoniazid via breast milk should receive supplemental pyridoxine.
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Exclusively breastfed infants receiving isoniazid via breast milk should receive supplemental pyridoxine: This statement refers to infants who are exclusively breastfed and are receiving isoniazid through breast milk because their mother is taking isoniazid as part of the standard 3-drug regimen for tuberculosis treatment. Isoniazid is an important component of tuberculosis treatment, but it can lead to a deficiency of vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) in both the mother and the infant. Vitamin B6 deficiency can cause peripheral neuropathy, which is a condition that affects the nerves and can lead to tingling, numbness, and weakness in the extremities. To prevent this potential side effect in the breastfeeding infant, it is recommended that infants receiving isoniazid through breast milk should receive supplemental pyridoxine (vitamin B6). By providing the infant with supplemental pyridoxine, the risk of vitamin B6 deficiency and peripheral neuropathy is reduced. Option C - If both the mother and infant have active pulmonary TB, they should be separated until the completion of 2 weeks of treatment: In the rare case of congenital TB (when both the mother and infant have active pulmonary TB), both should be started on treatment. The infant and mother need not be separated as long as both are adherent. Option D - Women taking isoniazid, rifampin, and ethambutol should not breastfeed due to potential toxicity to the infant: After at least two weeks of treatment for active tuberculosis, women can safely breastfeed. questions.answerText: Miglustat inhibits the synthesis of glucosylceramide.
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Miglustat inhibits the synthesis of glucosylceramide: Miglustat is a medication used in the treatment of Gaucher's disease, a rare genetic disorder characterized by a deficiency of the enzyme glucocerebrosidase. Glucocerebrosidase is responsible for breaking down glucosylceramide, a lipid that accumulates in Gaucher's disease. Miglustat functions by inhibiting the synthesis of glucosylceramide, which reduces the accumulation of this lipid in cells and alleviates the symptoms of Gaucher's disease. Incorrect Options: Option A - Miglustat enhances the activity of glucocerebrosidase: This option is incorrect because Miglustat does not enhance the activity of glucocerebrosidase. Instead, it works by a different mechanism, as explained above. Option B - Miglustat acts as a substrate for glucocerebrosidase: This option is incorrect because Miglustat is not a substrate for glucocerebrosidase. It does not serve as a molecule that the enzyme acts upon. Option D - Miglustat increases the production of glucocerebroside: This option is incorrect because Miglustat does not increase the production of glucocerebroside. Instead, it reduces the synthesis of glucosylceramide, which is a precursor to glucocerebroside. @Neet_pg_bot

He was diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis 2 months back and was started on anti-tuberculosis therapy. On examination, there is conjunctival pallor and dry lips with cracks at the angle of the mouth. Sensory examination shows decreased sensation of light touch and pinpricked in the lower limb, and motor examination is unremarkable. Hb: 9.8 g/dl
MCV: 72 femtoliter

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Pyridoxine : A deficiency of pyridoxine is associated with the development of paresthesias and sideroblastic/microcytic anaemia ( microcytic anaemia can cause cheilosis and glossitis) Patients taking anti-tubercular therapy (ATT) can develop pyridoxine deficiency due to isoniazid toxicity Pyridoxine is a co-factor that is required for the synthesis of neurotransmitters and the heme group of haemoglobin Hence deficiency of pyridoxine results in peripheral neuropathy, mainly affecting the sensations and anaemia Generally, pyridoxine deficiency is rare; however, in those patients who are taking ATT, isoniazid competes with pyridoxine in neurotransmitter synthesis To prevent pyridoxine deficiency due to isoniazid, supplemental pyridoxine is added as an adjuvant therapy In addition to that, INH is also associated with hepatotoxicity that presents with nausea, vomiting, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain Other relatively less common side effects of INH therapy are psychosis, optic neuritis, pellagra, metabolic acidosis, etc Incorrect Options: Option A - Folic acid : Folic acid deficiency gives rise to megaloblastic anaemia rather than microcytic or sideroblastic anaemia. Folic acid deficiency does not result in peripheral sensory neuropathy Option B - Vitamin B12: Vitamin B12 deficiency can lead to the development of peripheral neuropathy. However, in addition to peripheral neuropathy, other neurological manifestations are also present, i.e. ataxia, cognitive impairment, irritability, etc Vitamin B12 deficiency gives rise to macrocytic anaemia rather than microcytic anaemia Option C - Iron : Deficiency of iron results in microcytic anaemia However, iron deficiency is not associated with the development of neurological manifestations @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option D - Pyridoxine :

  • A deficiency of pyridoxine is associated with the development of paresthesias and sideroblastic/microcytic anaemia ( microcytic anaemia can cause cheilosis and glossitis)
  • Patients taking anti-tubercular therapy (ATT) can develop pyridoxine deficiency due to isoniazid toxicity 
  • Pyridoxine is a co-factor that is required for the synthesis of neurotransmitters and the heme group of haemoglobin 
  • Hence deficiency of pyridoxine results in peripheral neuropathy, mainly affecting the sensations and anaemia 
  • Generally, pyridoxine deficiency is rare; however, in those patients who are taking ATT, isoniazid competes with pyridoxine in neurotransmitter synthesis
  • To prevent pyridoxine deficiency due to isoniazid, supplemental pyridoxine is added as an adjuvant therapy 
  • In addition to that, INH is also associated with hepatotoxicity that presents with nausea, vomiting, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain
  • Other relatively less common side effects of INH therapy are psychosis, optic neuritis, pellagra, metabolic acidosis, etc

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Folic acid :

  • Folic acid deficiency gives rise to megaloblastic anaemia rather than microcytic or sideroblastic anaemia.
  • Folic acid deficiency does not result in peripheral sensory neuropathy 

Option B - Vitamin B12:

  • Vitamin B12 deficiency can lead to the development of peripheral neuropathy. However, in addition to peripheral neuropathy, other neurological manifestations are also present, i.e. ataxia, cognitive impairment, irritability, etc 
  • Vitamin B12 deficiency gives rise to macrocytic anaemia rather than microcytic anaemia

Option C - Iron :

  • Deficiency of iron results in microcytic anaemia 
  • However, iron deficiency is not associated with the development of neurological manifestations

On examination, a new murmur of mitral regurgitation is appreciated, and S1 and S2 are normal. Blood pressure 110/80 mmHg. Pulmonary auscultation shows fine end-inspiratory basilar crackles in both lungs. Jugular pulsation is not evident. questions.solution: Correct Option A- Congestive cardiac failure: The patient's presentation is consistent with acute pulmonary oedema due to congestive cardiac failure. Congestive heart failure is the inability of the heart to pump enough blood due to pathological changes in the myocardium to meet the metabolic requirements of the body. There are many causes of congestive cardiac failure; however, the most common and important are myocardial infarction, hypertension and diabetes mellitus. The patient presents with shortness of breath due to pulmonary congestion caused by impaired contractility of the heart leading to fluid build-up in the lungs. Orthopnoea (shortness of breath when lying flat) and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea (patient wakes up due to shortness of breath due to increased venous return). A new murmur of mitral regurgitation due to papillary muscle is the precipitating cause. On pulmonary auscultation, fine end-inspiratory basilar crackles in both lungs are highly characteristic. Incorrect Options: Option B- Pulmonary embolism: Pulmonary embolism also presents with sudden onset shortness of breath. However, the patient has thromboembolic risk factors such as recent surgery, prolonged immobilization, previously documented deep venous thrombosis, active cancer, paralysis, calf swelling, and varicose veins. Moreover, a chest X-ray shows Hampton Hump (a peripheral wedge-shaped opacity at the peripheral lung parenchyma caused by pulmonary infarction). Option C- Tension pneumothorax: Tension pneumothorax also presents with sudden severe shortness of breath. The presence of tracheal deviation and hyper resonant percussion with hemodynamic instability and the absence of broncho vascular markings on chest X-ray is suggestive of tension pneumothorax. It is a life-threatening condition in which the damaged tissue acts as a one-way valve in which the air enters the pleural cavity but cannot escape naturally, resulting in increased pressure into the pleural space, compressing the lung and mediastinum to the opposite side. Mediastinal deviation causes compression of the veins manifesting as jugular venous distension resulting in impaired venous return to the heart, manifesting as hemodynamic collapse (low blood pressure and tachycardia). Option D- Cardiac tamponade: Cardiac tamponade is an emergency caused by increased pericardial pressure due to pericardial effusion, which compresses the right ventricle. questions.stem: A 62-year-old male presents to the clinic complaining of pain and numbness in his lower legs while walking for a few blocks, which subsides after a few minutes of rest. The patient also reports a history of smoking for the past 40 years and hypertension for the past 15 years, which is currently well-controlled with medication. Physical examination reveals diminished pedal pulses bilaterally, with no signs of peripheral edema or ulceration. The patient denies any symptoms of claudication during a treadmill exercise test. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 62-year-old male presents to the clinic complaining of pain and numbness in his lower legs while walking for a few blocks, which subsides after a few minutes of rest. The patient also reports a history of smoking for the past 40 years and hypertension for the past 15 years, which is currently well-controlled with medication. Physical examination reveals diminished pedal pulses bilaterally, with no signs of peripheral edema or ulceration. The patient denies any symptoms of claudication during a treadmill exercise test. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- Chronic compartment syndrome: Chronic compartment syndrome is a disorder that causes pain and/or neurological problems because of impaired circulation and is characterized by recurring, transient pressure increases inside a fascial compartment. Athletes and military recruits participating in repeated physical exercise are likely to experience it in their lower legs. In this case, the presence of reduced pedal pulses bilaterally and the patient's feelings of discomfort and numbness in the lower legs that go away after a few minutes of rest point to the diagnosis of chronic compartment syndrome. Muscle aches, stiffness, weakness, and swelling are some of the symptoms, which are made worse by exercise and made better by rest. Also possible are paresthesia, numbness, and/or temporary nerve palsy (such as foot drop). The diagnosis is made using invasive compartment pressure measurements taken before and after exercise and symptoms that are consistently triggered by recurrent activity. To assess potential differential diagnoses, noninvasive testing methods including MRI, bone scintigraphy, and radiography may be performed. Conservative management, gait retraining, avoiding stimulating activities, and surgical fasciotomy are all possible forms of treatment. Incorrect Options: Option A- Diabetic neuropathy: Despite the fact that diabetic neuropathy can result in numbness and discomfort in the lower limbs, the patient's history of smoking, high blood pressure, and the presence of reduced pedal pulses on both sides point to a vascular rather than a neuropathic origin. Option B- Sciatica: Sciatica is a condition where the sciatic nerve is strained or irritated. The patient's symptoms are inconsistent with sciatica because they are not back-specific and do not grow worse with spinal movement. Option C- Venous insufficiency: Venous insufficiency can result in leg discomfort, edema, and skin changes; however, the patient's signs of pain and numbness that go away with rest and the existence of reduced pedal pulses on both sides point to an arterial rather than a venous origin. Moreover, venous insufficiency is not frequently diagnosed with a treadmill exercise test. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 68-year-old male is brought to the clinic with dyspnea and chest pain with mild exertion. He was diagnosed with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction two months ago. On physical examination, there are bilateral crackles in the lower lung fields. There is also the presence of a systolic murmur on auscultation. ECG shows deep Q waves in leads I, aVL, and V2-V5 with a 2-mm-ST segment elevation. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
questions.stemHtml: A 68-year-old male is brought to the clinic with dyspnea and chest pain with mild exertion. He was diagnosed with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction two months ago. On physical examination, there are bilateral crackles in the lower lung fields. There is also the presence of a systolic murmur on auscultation. ECG shows deep Q waves in leads I, aVL, and V2-V5 with a 2-mm-ST segment elevation. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Ventricular aneurysm: A ventricular aneurysm is one of the complications of STEMI. It causes progressive decompensated congestive heart failure. It can occur anywhere between day five-to-three-month post-MI. Generally, ST-segment elevation normalizes after a few weeks of a STEMI. Ventricular aneurysms present with persistent ST-segment elevation and deep Q-waves in the same leads. It leads to left ventricular enlargement and causes heart failure, angina, ventricular arrhythmias, functional mitral regurgitation, and mural thrombus with systemic embolization. Echocardiography can help to confirm the diagnosis of the ventricular aneurysm. Incorrect Options: Option A - Dressler’s syndrome: One of the complications of STEMI is late-onset post-MI pericarditis . It is also known as Dressler’s syndrome . It can usually develop after a week to a few months after STEMI. Clinical features of Dressler’s syndrome include fever, pleuritic chest pain, pericardial effusion, and rub. Dressler’s syndrome is believed to occur due to an autoimmune reaction to the antigens exposed because of myocardial infarction. ECG shows diffuse ST-segment elevation. Serosal surfaces such as lung pleura can also be involved , and it is generally treated with aspirin, NSAIDs, or glucocorticoids. This patient’s clinical features and ECG changes suggest a ventricular aneurysm. Option C - Papillary muscle rupture: Papillary muscle rupture is one of the fatal complications of STEMI. It occurs between day two and day seven post-MI. Patients with papillary muscle rupture present with hypotension, pulmonary oedema, and cardiogenic shock. This patient’s clinical features and ECG changes suggest a ventricular aneurysm. Option D - Ventricular free wall rupture: Ventricular free wall rupture causes sizeable pericardial effusion (friction rub). It presents with features of cardiac tamponade like hypotension, pulsus paradoxus, raised jugular pressure, and shortness of breath. This patient’s clinical features and ECG changes suggest a ventricular aneurysm. @Neet_pg_bot

By blocking the complement cascade at the C5 level, eculizumab prevents hemolysis and reduces the risk of thrombosis, the main complications of PNH. Option D - Upfront Allogeneic Stem Cell Transplantation: Allogeneic stem cell transplantation is the only curative option for PNH, but it is associated with significant risks and is typically reserved for cases with severe manifestations or those unresponsive to other treatments. questions.solution: Correct Option D - Prior to exercise, he needs to warm up and use a short-acting beta agonist: Exercise-induced asthma can occur in up to 20% of the general population and in up to 90% of those who have persistent asthma. Allergic rhinitis is a strongly associated factor, and atopy is even more strongly associated. It usually occurs after approximately 3-8 minutes of exercise and peaks with symptoms at around 15 minutes. Symptoms resolve spontaneously by 60 minutes. Pathophysiology is unclear, however, it may be related to “airway cooling” in which a dry mucosal and increased surface osmolality can trigger a mast cell release of inflammatory mediators. A “thermal” hypothesis proposes that airway cooling followed by rapid rewarming can cause airway vascular congestion with increased permeability that gives rise to edema and obstruction of the airway. Treatment of choice: warm up and use a short-acting beta agonist. questions.solution: Correct Option C - Intravenous octreotide: Esophageal varices form at a rate of 5 to 15 percent per year in patients with cirrhosis, with one-third of patients with varices developing variceal hemorrhage. On postoperative day 2, she complained of nausea, dizziness, and a headache. A complete neurological exam is unremarkable. A metabolic panel is significant for hypernatremia only. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this hypernatremia?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Neurosurgery: This patient underwent neurosurgery, and the surgeon suspected damage to the hypothalamus. The hypothalamus has many functions. One of these functions is the anti-diuretic hormone (ADH) production. ADH is responsible for the reabsorption of free water in the kidneys. ADH is produced in the hypothalamus and stored in the posterior pituitary gland before releasing into the bloodstream. Damage to the hypothalamus is one of the causes of central diabetes insipidus (DI), a condition characterized by an absence of ADH. In central DI, there is free water loss from the kidneys due to the absence of ADH. This causes concentration of the contents of the blood. One of the main electrolyte imbalances caused by central DI is hypernatremia. All the features in this scenario are suggestive of central DI. Incorrect Options: Option A - Intravenous fluid therapy: It is possible to cause hypernatremia through the administration of intravenous fluids. But, this is possible if the fluids used are hypertonic. The patient in this scenario received isotonic fluids. Therefore it is unlikely that intravenous fluid therapy is the culprit. Option B - Fluid loss from surgical trauma: The fluid lost due to surgical trauma is generally isotonic. Isotonic fluid loss is unlikely to cause electrolyte imbalances. This is because the blood becomes neither concentrated nor diluted. If a significant fluid loss does occur, there is a physiologic release of ADH and aldosterone. Aldosterone causes the reabsorption of salt and fluid. The net effect may be seen as a slight dilution of blood, but it is unlikely to cause hypernatremia, as in this case. Option D - None of the above: There are clear features suggestive of a diagnosis of central DI. @Neet_pg_bot

Despite initial supportive measures, the patient's hypoxemia persists. Which of the following pharmacologic interventions has been shown to improve mortality in ARDS?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Inhaled nitric oxide: In patients with severe ARDS, inhaled nitric oxide (iNO) has been shown to improve oxygenation by selectively dilating pulmonary vasculature, thereby improving ventilation-perfusion matching. However, it's important to note that while iNO improves oxygenation, its impact on mortality in ARDS is not consistently demonstrated in all studies. It is generally reserved for cases with persistent hypoxemia despite other supportive measures. Incorrect Options: Option A- Inhaled corticosteroids: Inhaled corticosteroids have not been proven to improve mortality in ARDS. Systemic corticosteroids are sometimes used in certain cases but are not the first-line treatment for ARDS and may have variable effects on outcomes. Option B- High-dose systemic corticosteroids: High-dose systemic corticosteroids have not shown consistent mortality benefits in ARDS and may be associated with adverse effects. They are not recommended as routine therapy in ARDS. Option D- Intravenous vitamin C: While some studies have suggested potential benefits of intravenous vitamin C in ARDS, evidence is not robust, and its routine use is not well-established. Further research is needed to determine its role in clinical management. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty (PTA): The patient presents with the ‘string of beads’ appearance suggesting a diagnosis of fibromuscular dysplasia. Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD ) is a non-inflammatory arterial disease characterised by abnormal smooth muscle cell proliferation within the arterial wall , resulting in arterial stenosis, aneurysm formation, or dissection. Physical examination reveals elevated blood pressure and a bruit over the affected blood vessel. Laboratory findings include: Elevated creatinine level ( in cases of renal artery involvement ) Elevated plasma renin activity (in cases of renal artery involvement ) MRI findings show: "String-of-beads" appearance in the affected artery Arterial stenosis, aneurysm, or dissection Treatment involves: Blood pressure control with medication such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or calcium channel blockers In cases of renal artery involvement, percutaneous transluminal angioplasty (PTA) with or without stenting is a management option . In cases of carotid artery involvement, carotid endarterectomy or stenting is advisable. Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty is a minimally invasive procedure. It is a safe and effective treatment option for patients with fibromuscular dysplasia with severe or symptomatic renal artery stenosis. It improves blood pressure control, reduces the risk of renal failure, and improves the quality of life. ACEIs and ARBs are the preferred antihypertensive agents in patients with renal artery stenosis as they can help to reduce proteinuria and slow the progression of renal disease. In patients with severe stenosis or renal artery dissection causing renal artery stenosis, medical management alone may not be sufficient to control blood pressure and prevent further renal damage. Option C - Surgical revascularization: It is a more invasive and complex procedure than PTA. The patient in this scenario has severe bilateral renal artery stenosis with elevated creatinine levels indicating renal impairment, which may increase the risk of complications from surgical revascularization. It may not be feasible or appropriate for all patients with renal artery stenosis, particularly those not good candidates for surgery due to underlying medical conditions. options.label: B
options.text: Doxorubicin, bleomycin (low dose), vinblastine, dacarbazine, ± irradiation

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Brentuximab vedotin plus (AVD): New drugs, such as brentuximab vedotin plus AVD, have had their efficacies demonstrated in relapsed/refractory HL may be more appropriate in refractory patients with treatment-related pulmonary fibrosis. In addition, initiation therapy with brentuximab vedotin plus AVD resulted in statistically significant increase in survival in addition to a decrease in pulmonary toxicities. This regimen would be particularly appropriate in elderly patients, who are at an even higher risk of bleomycin induced pulmonary toxicity. Incorrect Options: Option A - Doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, dacarbazine (ABVD), ± irradiation: The ABVD regimen is a standard chemotherapy protocol used for the treatment of Hodgkin's lymphoma. While it has been effective in many cases, it includes bleomycin, which is associated with a significant risk of pulmonary toxicity, especially in patients with pre-existing lung conditions like pulmonary fibrosis. Using bleomycin in patients with treatment-related pulmonary fibrosis could exacerbate the lung condition and lead to severe adverse effects. Therefore, ABVD is not the most appropriate choice for this patient. Option B - Doxorubicin, bleomycin (low dose), vinblastine, dacarbazine, ± irradiation: This option attempts to reduce the risk of bleomycin-induced pulmonary toxicity by using a low dose of bleomycin. However, even at low doses, bleomycin can still cause significant lung toxicity, especially in patients with compromised lung function like those with treatment-related pulmonary fibrosis. Hence, using bleomycin, even at a low dose, might not be the best approach for this patient. Option C - Doxorubicin, vinblastine, dacarbazine, ± irradiation: This option removes bleomycin from the regimen, which can indeed decrease the risk of bleomycin-induced pulmonary toxicity. However, the omission of bleomycin might lead to suboptimal efficacy in treating Hodgkin's lymphoma, as bleomycin is an essential component of most Hodgkin's lymphoma treatment regimens.
