questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old male presents with palpitations and shortness of breath started a few minutes ago at a concert. She reports a history of palpitations on exertion in the past but never to this extent. On examination, her blood pressure is 128/76 mmHg, and her heart rate is 220/min with a regular rhythm. His ECG shows a narrow complex tachycardia with a regular rhythm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- Atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia (AVRT): The patient's symptoms and ECG findings are consistent with the diagnosis of AVRT, a type of supraventricular tachycardia caused by an abnormal accessory pathway between the atria and ventricles. During AVRT, there is a re-entry circuit between the AV node and the accessory pathway, causing a narrow complex tachycardia with a regular rhythm. The delta wave on the ECG represents the premature activation of the ventricles via the accessory pathway, resulting in a shortened PR interval. questions.solution: Correct Option D- Acute Viral infection: This patient’s clinical symptoms point toward the diagnosis of acute pericarditis. The most common etiology for this condition is a viral infection. Hence, the correct answer is option D. The symptoms in this patient like chest pain that worsens with inspiration and is relieved on leaning forward, nausea (due to irritation of the phrenic nerve that innervates the pericardium, high-pitched rubbing sound during systole (pericardial friction rub – best heard during expiration), characteristic ECG are indicative of acute pericarditis. Of all the given etiologies, acute viral infection is the most common cause of pericarditis. A large number of cases are also labeled idiopathic but these are assumed to be secondary to asymptomatic viral infection. Following the idiopathic etiology, the second most common is confirmed viral etiology. The presence of myalgia in this patient point to a possible influenza virus infection which is often found with myalgia. Other etiologies can include bacterial or fungal infections, myocardial infarction, radiation exposure, chemotherapy, or uremia. Incorrect Options: Option A- Acute myocardial infarction: Acute myocardial infarction does not present with chest pain that changes with position. ECG does not show diffuse ST elevation. The elevation would be limited to a few contiguous leads in case of acute myocardial infarction. Pericarditis can develop secondary to myocardial infarction but this patient lacks any risk factors of myocardial infarction and seems unlikely to develop it. Option B- Systemic Lupus Erythematosus: It is common for a patient to develop cardiac complications in systemic lupus erythematosus. However, pericarditis in such cases is usually subclinical and overlaps with endocarditis, seen only on an echocardiogram. Moreover, this patient shows no signs of systemic lupus erythematosus. Option C- Dressler Syndrome: This is a complication of myocardial infarction in which an autoimmune reaction post-infarction results in pericarditis. questions.stem: A 30-year-old male complained of dizziness, palpitations, syncope and labored breathing, especially at night. ECG showed ST elevation in lead V1-V3 with right bundle branch block and normal QT interval. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis of this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 30-year-old male complained of dizziness, palpitations, syncope and labored breathing, especially at night. ECG showed ST elevation in lead V1-V3 with right bundle branch block and normal QT interval. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis of this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Brugada syndrome: This patient’s ECG findings are consistent with Brugada syndrome, a genetic disorder. Patients with Brugada syndrome may present with polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. It is an autosomal dominant disorder that occurs commonly in Asian males . Patients with Brugada syndrome have defective sodium channel function . On ECG, there will be a pseudo-right bundle branch block and ST elevation in lead V1-V3. There will be no prolongation of the QT interval. The risk of sudden cardiac death in these patients is only prevented with implantable cardioverter-defibrillator. Incorrect Options: Option A - Romano-Ward syndrome: Romano-Ward syndrome is a congenital long QT syndrome. In Romano-Ward syndrome, myocardial repolarisation occurs due to ion channel defects. Mostly it occurs due to loss-of-function mutations that affect the K+ channels. These patients have an increased risk of death due to torsades de pointes. Option B - Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome: Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome is a congenital long QT syndrome. In Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome , myocardial repolarisation occurs due to ion channel defects. Mostly it occurs due to loss-of-function mutations that affect the K+ channels. These patients have an increased risk of death due to torsades de pointes . It is similar in presentation to Romano-Ward syndrome, but these patients also have sensorineural deafness . Option C - Sick sinus syndrome: This patient’s presentation is inconsistent with sick sinus syndrome. Sick sinus syndrome is usually present in older age but can also occur in young patients. It occurs due to ischemia, fibrosis, or degenerative changes in the SA node . Typically, the patient presents with dizzy spells, palpitations, or syncope due to intermittent tachycardia and bradycardia. ECG will have absent ventricular or atrial activity (Sinus arrest or SA block). @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 4 year-old female with sickle cell disease presents with fever, cough and chest pain. She is alert and following commands but is in moderate respiratory distress. She is breathing 40 times per minute, and her oxygen saturation is 89%. Chest X-ray reveals diffuse, bilateral consolidations. Her hemoglobin level is 11 grams/dL. In addition to empiric antibiotics, which of the following therapies should be utilized in her care?
questions.stemHtml: A 4 year-old female with sickle cell disease presents with fever, cough and chest pain. She is alert and following commands but is in moderate respiratory distress. She is breathing 40 times per minute, and her oxygen saturation is 89%. Chest X-ray reveals diffuse, bilateral consolidations. Her hemoglobin level is 11 grams/dL. In addition to empiric antibiotics, which of the following therapies should be utilized in her care?

options.label: A
options.text: 60 mL/kg bolus of normal saline followed by an infusion at two times the maintenance rate

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Exchange Transfusion: Acute chest syndrome is the leading cause of death in patients with sickle cell disease. It is most common in young children, and the incidence decreases with age. Classic signs and symptoms include fever, cough, wheezing, and chest pain. Chest X-rays commonly reveal patchy infiltrates. It is important to note that X-ray findings commonly lag behind patients’ symptoms. While the patient is in some respiratory distress, she is alert and protecting her airway. Supplemental oxygen and possibly non-invasive positive pressure ventilation should be trialed before considering intubation. Exchange transfusion may be lifesaving in cases of severe crises. It seems to provide the most benefit to patients with Hb levels >9 grams/dL. The procedure removes sickled cells and replaces them with normal ones with the goal of reversing vasooclusion and improving blood flow. Incorrect Options: Option A - 60 mL/kg bolus of normal saline followed by an infusion at two times the maintenance rate: IV fluids have classically been used in the management of sickle cell crises, however more recent evidence has shown little utility to the practice. Aggressive fluid resuscitation may in fact cause pulmonary edema and worsen lung function. Option C - Immediate Endotracheal Intubation: Supplemental oxygen and possibly non-invasive positive pressure ventilation should be trialed before considering intubation. Option D - Parenteral Corticosteroids: There is no indication for corticosteroids in the management of acute chest syndrome @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following is a common adverse effect of acyclovir therapy that requires close monitoring?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is a common adverse effect of acyclovir therapy that requires close monitoring?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Renal failure: The adverse effect of acyclovir with the greatest morbidity is crystal-induced nephrotoxicity due to crystallization of the drug within the nephron. Acyclovir has low solubility in urine and therefore it is very important to ensure that patients are not intravascularly depleted as this complication of acyclovir therapy is much higher in patients that are volume contracted. Incorrect Options: Option A - Thrombocytopenia: Thrombocytopenia refers to a low platelet count, which can result in an increased risk of bleeding. Acyclovir is not typically associated with thrombocytopenia as an adverse effect. This option is not a common adverse effect of acyclovir therapy and does not require close monitoring specifically for this drug. Option B - Liver Failure: Liver failure involves the severe impairment of liver function. Acyclovir is primarily eliminated by the kidneys, and significant liver toxicity is not a common adverse effect of acyclovir therapy. While liver function tests might be monitored in some cases, liver failure is not a typical concern with acyclovir use. Option D - Pancytopenia : Pancytopenia refers to a decrease in all three major blood cell types: red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Acyclovir is not typically associated with pancytopenia. This option is not a common adverse effect of acyclovir therapy and does not require specific monitoring for this drug. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 73-year-old female presents to your clinic with early stage (Lugano I) H. Pylori positive, gastric MALT lymphoma. Which of the following is a translocation commonly seen in gastric MALT lymphoma, that can affect the therapy?
questions.stemHtml: A 73-year-old female presents to your clinic with early stage (Lugano I) H. Pylori positive, gastric MALT lymphoma. Which of the following is a translocation commonly seen in gastric MALT lymphoma, that can affect the therapy?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - t(11;18): This translocation involves the genes API2 (also known as BIRC3) and MALT1. It is the most common genetic abnormality seen in gastric MALT lymphoma. The t(11;18) translocation leads to the formation of an API2-MALT1 fusion protein, which can activate certain signaling pathways and promote cell survival. Patients with this translocation may have a less favorable response to standard H. pylori eradication therapy and may require alternative treatments. Incorrect Options: Option B - t(2;13): This translocation is not commonly associated with gastric MALT lymphoma. It is more frequently found in other types of lymphoma, such as mantle cell lymphoma, where it involves the CCND1 gene on chromosome 11 and the IgH locus on chromosome 14. Option C - t(14;18): This translocation is known as the t(14;18)(q32;q21) translocation, which is commonly associated with follicular lymphoma but not gastric MALT lymphoma. It involves the BCL2 gene on chromosome 18 and the IgH locus on chromosome 14. Option D - t(8;14): This translocation is typically associated with Burkitt lymphoma, a high-grade B-cell lymphoma, and is not commonly seen in gastric MALT lymphoma. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: In regard to high-altitude acclimatization, which of the following is an expected physiologic response?
questions.stemHtml: In regard to high-altitude acclimatization, which of the following is an expected physiologic response?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Erythropoietin secretion: Erythropoietin is secreted in response to hypoxemia, which in turn stimulates the production of red blood cells, leading to new circulatory red blood cells in 4-5 days. In response to high altitude, the peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid bodies respond to a decrease in PaO 2 and signal the respiratory control center to increase ventilation. As ventilation increases, a respiratory alkalosis occurs that acts as negative feedback on the central respiratory centre. The release of catecholamines on ascent stimulates the circulatory system to increase cardiac output (elevated heart rate and elevated blood pressure). Incorrect Options: Option B - Respiratory acidosis: This is not an expected physiologic response to high-altitude acclimatization. At high altitudes, the body experiences a respiratory alkalosis due to hyperventilation in response to hypoxia. Option C - Decreased blood pressure: At high altitudes, the body tends to respond to hypoxia by increasing sympathetic activity and releasing catecholamines. This can lead to an increase in blood pressure, not a decrease. Option D - Pulmonary artery hypotension: At high altitudes, hypoxia can actually lead to pulmonary artery hypertension, not hypotension. The body's response to hypoxia includes vasoconstriction of pulmonary vessels, leading to increased pulmonary artery pressures. This is a compensatory mechanism to improve oxygenation. @Neet_pg_bot

A physical evaluation reveals tenderness in the right flank and the abdomen. On ultrasonography, the right ureter and renal pelvis are distended. Which of the following best describes the state of this patient's underlying cause?
questions.stemHtml: A 68-year-old man visits the doctor to have his right flank pain examined. He has a history of coronary artery disease and diabetes. His BP is 160/90 mm Hg. A physical evaluation reveals tenderness in the right flank and the abdomen. On ultrasonography, the right ureter and renal pelvis are distended. Which of the following best describes the state of this patient's underlying cause?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Common iliac artery aneurysm: Right flank tenderness , abdominal discomfort , and hypertension are all signs of urinary tract obstruction that can eventually result in hydronephrosis in this patient. As it travels from the kidney to the bladder, the centre section of the ureter passes anterior to the common iliac artery . Large aneurysms of the common, external, or internal iliac arteries can constrict the ureter , leading to an extrinsic urinary tract obstruction and unilateral hydronephrosis , though these cases are uncommon. Incorrect Options: Option B - Renal artery stenosis: Renal ischemia and decreased blood flow to the kidneys are possible effects of renal artery stenosis . Insufficient blood supply also activates the renin angiotensin aldosterone system (RAAS) , which results in hypertension. However, abdominal or right flank pain wouldn't caused on by renal artery stenosis. Additionally, it is not recognized as a cause of hydronephrosis. Option C - Diabetic nephropathy: Renal failure can follow from decreased GFR due to long-term, uncontrolled diabetes. It is caused microscopic albuminuria resulting in nephrotic syndrome. It is uncommon for chronic renal failure to result in flank or abdominal pain. Hydronephrosis is caused by obstruction to the urinary flow, it is not caused by diabetic nephropathy. Option D - Benign prostatic hyperplasia: The urethra connects the prostate to the bladder. As seen in BPH, enlargement of the prostate can cause urethral blockage , leading to bladder outlet obstruction. Patients with BPH usually present with urinary frequency, urgency, and urge incontinence rather than abdominal pain. Furthermore, this obstruction would result in bilateral, rather than unilateral, hydronephrosis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A- Oral Atenolol: The signs and symptoms of this patient suggest a stable coronary artery disease (CAD). Stable coronary artery disease is a type of coronary artery disease in which there are pathological atherosclerotic changes in the coronary vessel walls. Patients are either asymptomatic or have stable or low-risk unstable angina with normal ECG and normal cardiac markers. It is also used to characterize patients with a previous myocardial infarction whose symptoms are controlled with treatment. A first-line treatment for individuals with stable CAD, Atenolol , is a beta 1-selective adrenergic receptor blocker that improves exercise tolerance and decreases the frequency of anginal episodes. Like other beta-blockers, Atenolol lowers heart rate and cardiac contractility, lowering myocardial oxygen demand and alleviating anginal discomfort. The rise in coronary vascular resistance that results from beta-blockers inhibition of adrenergic-mediated coronary vasodilation is offset by the lower heart rate, which increases coronary perfusion by lengthening diastole. Risk-reducing measures (secondary prevention of CAD) include weight reduction, quitting smoking, aerobic exercise, and pharmaceutical treatment (which includes antiplatelet therapy, lipid-lowering therapy, and management of hypertension and diabetes). If there are contraindications to beta-blockers or if beta-blockers do not sufficiently manage symptoms, alternative antianginal agents are calcium channel blockers, long-acting nitrates (such as isosorbide mononitrate), and ranolazine. Incorrect Options: Option B- low dose aspirin: Aspirin inhibits COX-1 irreversibly , which prevents platelet aggregation. Antiplatelet therapy lowers the chance of complications from stable angina (e.g., myocardial infarction). It is recommended for all patients with ischemic heart disease who do not have particular contraindications to antiplatelet drugs. However, aspirin therapy does not improve exercise tolerance or decrease anginal pain in patients with stable angina. Option C- Percutaneous coronary angiography: Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is typically used to diagnose and manage the acute coronary syndrome. In stable angina, as seen here, PCI is only indicated if there are activity-limiting symptoms despite optimal medical treatment, contraindications to medical therapy, or stenosis of multiple coronary arteries (e.g., left coronary artery), none of which are present in this patient. Option D- Sublingual nitroglycerin: To increase coronary perfusion and lower cardiac oxygen demand, nitroglycerin , a short-acting nitrate, dilates the coronary vasculature and lowers left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (preload). In individuals with stable ischemic heart disease , it may decrease anginal symptoms. Nitroglycerin is a first-line treatment for alleviating acute angina symptoms but does not increase endurance during prolonged activity. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C - His condition is permanent: This patient has post-viral gastroparesis. This is seen with various viral illnesses including Epstein-Barr virus and cytomegalovirus infection. The illness can have 2 courses: it can resolve slowly over a year or be more prolonged. Typically, if there is no involvement of the autonomic neurologic system, the symptoms will slowly resolve over the course of a year. However, for those with involvement of their autonomic nervous system, the symptoms can take several years to resolve. However, they are not permanent. There is no role for anti-viral therapy at this time. Incorrect Options: Option A - It can be seen with Epstein-Barr virus infection: This is a correct statement. The patient's symptoms, which began after a benign illness, could be associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection. EBV is known to cause infectious mononucleosis, which presents with symptoms like nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fevers, and can lead to persistent symptoms in some cases. Option B - His autonomic nervous system was affected: This is a correct statement. The patient's symptoms of recurrent nausea, vomiting, and early satiety could be indicative of autonomic nervous system dysfunction. The autonomic nervous system controls involuntary functions like digestion, and its involvement can lead to gastrointestinal symptoms. Option D - There is no role for anti-viral therapy: This is a correct statement. In cases of autonomic nervous system dysfunction or post-infectious syndromes like post-infectious gastroparesis, anti-viral therapy is generally not the primary treatment. questions.solution: Correct Option B- Increased upper airway muscle tone: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) is characterized by repetitive episodes of upper airway obstruction during sleep, leading to complete or partial cessation of airflow (apneas) or a reduction in airflow (hypopneas). The primary pathophysiological mechanism in OSA involves a loss of upper airway muscle tone during sleep, particularly in the pharyngeal muscles. This results in collapse or narrowing of the upper airway, leading to obstructed breathing. Incorrect Options: Option A- Decreased central respiratory drive: OSA is not primarily caused by a decrease in central respiratory drive. In fact, individuals with OSA often have an increased drive to breathe due to the hypoxia and hypercapnia resulting from repeated apneas. Option C- Impaired lung compliance: OSA is primarily a disorder of upper airway obstruction rather than impaired lung compliance. Lung compliance refers to the ease with which the lungs can expand, and it is not the primary issue in OSA. Option D- Loss of lung elasticity: Loss of lung elasticity is not the primary mechanism in OSA. OSA is characterized by upper airway obstruction, and lung elasticity primarily relates to the ability of the lungs to recoil during expiration. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 17-year-old female with a diagnosis of type III von Willebrand disease is admitted to the hospital with a lower G.I. bleed. Hemoglobin has dropped from a baseline of 9.8 g/dL to 6.2 g/dL. Patient is given 3 units of packed red blood cells. Which of the following would be the least appropriate therapy ?
questions.stemHtml: A 17-year-old female with a diagnosis of type III von Willebrand disease is admitted to the hospital with a lower G.I. bleed. Hemoglobin has dropped from a baseline of 9.8 g/dL to 6.2 g/dL. Patient is given 3 units of packed red blood cells. Which of the following would be the least appropriate therapy ?
questions.solution: Correct Option - DDAVP (Desmopressin): DDAVP (Desmopressin) is not an appropriate therapy for patients with type III von Willebrand disease. Type III von Willebrand disease is characterized by a complete deficiency of von Willebrand factor (vWF). Unlike patients with type I or type II von Willebrand disease, patients with type III lack the necessary storage pool of vWF in endothelial cells or megakaryocytes. DDAVP works by releasing stored vWF from endothelial cells, which can then aid in hemostasis. Since patients with type III von Willebrand disease have no stored vWF, DDAVP is not effective in increasing vWF levels in these individuals. Therefore, DDAVP is not a suitable treatment option for type III von Willebrand disease, and other therapies should be considered. Incorrect Options: Option A - Recombinant von Willebrand factor: Recombinant von Willebrand factor (rVWF) replacement therapy is a suitable and effective treatment option for patients with type III von Willebrand disease. It provides the missing von Willebrand factor, helping to correct the bleeding disorder. Option C - Fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate: Fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate contain clotting factors, including von Willebrand factor. They can be used in the treatment of bleeding episodes in patients with type III von Willebrand disease. However, the use of these products may not be as controlled or convenient as recombinant von Willebrand factor. Option D - Aminocaproic acid: Aminocaproic acid is an antifibrinolytic agent that can help prevent the breakdown of clots. It is sometimes used as an adjunctive therapy in patients with bleeding disorders. While it can be considered as part of the treatment plan, it is not typically the primary therapy for type III von Willebrand disease. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 34-year-old female in her 24th week of gestation is referred for the treatment of active tuberculosis. Drug-resistance testing results are within normal limits. As you design a treatment regimen, which of the following anti-tuberculosis drugs should you avoid prescribing due to an unacceptable level of risk in pregnancy?
questions.solution: Correct Option A – Streptomycin : Streptomycin is contraindicated during pregnancy and, in addition to amikacin, results in damage to the vestibular nerve during the development of the fetus. Additional anti-tuberculosis medications that are contraindicated during pregnancy include ethionamide, capreomycin, kanamycin, pyrazinamide, and cycloserine . The dilemma in some cases is that these second-line drugs are sometimes needed to treat multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, which is challenging to treat during pregnancy. Incorrect Options: Option B – Rifampin: Rifampin, ethambutol, and isoniazid comprise the recommended 3-drug regimen for the treatment of active tuberculosis in pregnancy. In cases in which hepatitis and neuropathy related to isoniazid are a concern, clarithromycin is often used as a substitute for isoniazid in pregnancy. Of the drugs in the usual regimen for pregnancy, isoniazid is often the best tolerated. questions.stem: A 15-year-old African American boy presented to the clinic after an episode of gross hematuria. He has a history of excessive urination and wakes 2-3 times at night for urination. His physical examination shows no abnormalities. His mother died of a stroke when he was 2 years of age. Urinalysis show’s following: Specific gravity 1.005 Protein None Blood Moderate Red blood cells Many/hpf Which part of the kidney is affected in this patient?
questions.stemHtml:
A 15-year-old African American boy presented to the clinic after an episode of gross hematuria. He has a history of excessive urination and wakes 2-3 times at night for urination. His physical examination shows no abnormalities. His mother died of a stroke when he was 2 years of age. Urinalysis show’s following:
			Specific gravity
			1.005
			Protein
			None
			Blood
			Moderate
			Red blood cells
			Many/hpf
Which part of the kidney is affected in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Renal papillae This patient presents with gross hematuria with complaints of polyuria with a low urine specific gravity consistent with hyposthenuria and the inability of the kidneys to concentrate urine, a feature of sickle cell disease. His family history is significant for early-onset stroke, which can be a severe complication of sickle cell disease (SCD) due to cerebrovascular occlusion from sickling. However, he has no other symptoms. Therefore, sickle cell trait (SCT) is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms. Sickle cell trait is a benign condition associated with hemoglobin AS that is more common in Africa, the Middle East, and Mediterranean countries and African American and Hispanic individuals. Hyposthenuria is common in patients with SCD and may also develop in those with SCT. In response to hypoxic, hyperosmolar conditions of the renal medulla, red blood cells sickle in the vasa recta, impairing free water reabsorption and countercurrent exchange. Patients typically have polyuria and nocturia despite fluid restriction. Urine osmolality is low; however, normal serum sodium is maintained due to intact antidiuretic hormone (ADH). Urinary diluting capacity is also intact as it is a function of the superficial loop of Henle, which is not supplied by the vasa recta. Non-glomerular hematuria is characterized by gross hematuria with normal-appearing red blood cells (RBCs) but without significant proteinuria. Etiologies include: Cancer (e.g. renal cell, prostate) Infections (e.g. cystitis) Polycystic kidney disease Nephrolithiasis Papillary necrosis Gross hematuria can be from: Bladder (e.g. cystitis. cancer) Renal (e.g. glomerulonephritis) Ureteral pathology (e.g. nephrolithiasis) Prostate pathology (e.g. benign prostatic hyperplasia) This patient's gross hematuria and urinalysis with normal-appearing red blood cells (RBCs) suggest an extra-glomerular etiology. Painless hematuria is likely due to renal papillary ischemia or necrosis. The relatively low local partial pressure of oxygen in the vasa recta predisposes the affected red blood cells to sickle. Papillary necrosis can occur with massive hematuria, but the episodes are usually mild and resolve spontaneously. The urinalysis usually shows normal-appearing RBCs. It may be associated with sickle cell disease/trait. Other renal complications include: Hyposthenuria; inability to concentrate the urine (vasa recta damage with an inability to maintain concentrated medullary gradient) Distal renal tubular acidosis (tubular damage with impaired H+ secretion). Incorrect options: Option B: Renal interstitium The renal interstitium refers to the connective tissue and extracellular matrix that comprise the space between the renal tubules and blood vessels in the kidney. The interstitium plays an important role in regulating renal function by providing support and structural organization for the various components of the kidney. One of the primary functions of the renal interstitium is to maintain the integrity of the renal tubules and blood vessels. The interstitium contains collagen fibers and other extracellular matrix components that support and help maintain the structural integrity of the kidney. The interstitium also contains various cells, including fibroblasts and macrophages, involved in tissue repair and immune defense. The interstitium is also important for regulating fluid and electrolyte balance in the kidney. The interstitial fluid communicates with the blood and the tubular fluid, exchanging ions and solutes between these compartments. The interstitium is also involved in the production and secretion of various hormones and growth factors that regulate renal function. Renal tumors or malignancies (e.g., renal cell cancer) involving the interstitium can present as non-glomerular hematuria. However, isosthenuria would not be typically seen with this condition. Option C: Glomerulus The glomerulus is a specialized structure in the kidney that plays a critical role in blood filtration and urine production. It is a small, spherical structure composed of a network of capillaries, known as glomerular capillaries, that is surrounded by a layer of specialized cells called podocytes. The glomerular capillaries are highly permeable, allowing water and small solutes to pass through the Bowman's capsule, the first part of the renal tubule. The podocytes, which have unique finger-like projections called foot processes, form a barrier that helps to regulate the passage of larger molecules, such as proteins, into the Bowman's capsule. Blood filtration in the glomerulus is regulated by complex interactions between the podocytes, mesangial cells, and the blood vessels that supply the glomerulus. These interactions help to maintain the proper balance of fluid and solutes in the body while preventing the loss of important molecules such as proteins. Glomerular hematuria refers to the presence of red blood cells in the urine that originate from the glomerulus in the kidney. This condition can be caused by several different physiological factors, which are as follows: Damage to the glomerular capillaries, e.g. glomerulonephritis, lupus nephritis, and vasculitis. Abnormalities in the structure or function of the glomerular filtration barrier, e.g. Alport syndrome. Abnormalities in platelet function or coagulation, e.g. thrombotic microangiopathy. Diseases of the glomerulus cause microscopic hematuria, though gross hematuria may be present in some cases. It is usually due to glomerulonephritis (GN or basement membrane disease. Symptoms are usually absent or nonspecific (e.g., low back pain), and patients may present after developing features of the nephritic syndrome (e.g., hematuria, hypertension, oliguria, elevated creatinine). Urinalysis usually shows proteinuria with dysmorphic RBCs or RBC casts. Option D: Renal Tubules Renal tubules are the microscopic tubes in the kidney that filter blood and produce urine. They are located in the nephrons, the kidney's functional units. The renal tubules comprise several distinct segments, each with a unique structure and function. Hematuria caused by the renal tubules, also known as tubular hematuria, refers to the presence of red blood cells in the urine originating from the kidney tubules. Causes of tubular hematuria include: Damage to the renal tubules, e.g. interstitial nephritis, polycystic kidney disease, and certain medications. Kidney stones. Bleeding disorders, such as von Willebrand disease or thrombocytopenia. Acute tubular necrosis is characterized by acute azotemia following a hypotensive or nephrotoxic injury. Patients may have dark or cola-coloured urine, but significant hematuria is uncommon. Tubulointerstitial nephritis causes microscopic hematuria associated with elevated creatinine and variable proteinuria. It is most commonly due to certain medications, including antibiotics, NSAIDs, and diuretics. @Neet_pg_bot

What would be the recommended first-line management?
questions.stemHtml: A patient with a newly diagnosed diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (SSC), undergoes screening with an upper GI endoscopy, 24 hours - ambulatory pH monitoring and oesophageal manometry, which show features of reflux oesophagitis and lower oesophageal dysmotility; however, the patient is completely asymptomatic. What would be the recommended first-line management?

options.label: B
options.text: Lifestyle modifications and regular proton pump inhibitor

options.label: C
options.text: Lifestyle modifications and PRN (as and when required) antacids

questions.answerText: Lifestyle modifications and regular proton pump inhibitor
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Lifestyle modifications and regular proton pump inhibitor: The routine screening for oesophageal abnormalities during the initial presentation is, therefore, recommended. Gastro-oesophageal reflux in SSC patients is managed with behavioural modifications in addition to long-term, high-dose proton pump inhibition (PPI) to reduce gastric acid secretion. Smoking cessation, elevation of the head off the bed and avoiding eating in the hours before retiring are generally recommended lifestyle modifications. Incorrect Options: Option A - Lifestyle modifications only: Lifestyle modifications alone are insufficient and PPIs should be offered to patients as first-line treatment. Option C - Lifestyle modifications and PRN (as and when required) antacids: As and when required (PRN) use of antacid alone with lifestyle changes are not recommended as first-line. Option D - Lifestyle modifications and regular domperidone: Domperidone can be used for reflux and to aid motility, but regular PPI therapy would be the recommended first-line therapy. @Neet_pg_bot

What is the most likely cause of the acid-base abnormality?
questions.solution: Correct Option A- Increased ketones in the blood: Polyuria, polydipsia, nausea, vomiting, volume depletion (such as dry oral mucosa, decreased skin turgor), mental status abnormalities, and coma are among the clinical characteristics of Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA). Abdominal pain, hyperventilation, and a fruity stench to the breath are common in DKA. Diabetes patients with type 1 diabetes are more likely to experience diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), which occurs when there isn't enough insulin to stop lipolysis, leading to ketone production and acidosis. Increased ketones such as Beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate disrupt the pH towards the acidic environment i.e., less than 7.35. The first step in assessing metabolic acidosis is the anion gap calculation. The total concentration of cations must be close to the concentration of anions to maintain electrical neutrality. The discrepancy between the concentration of measured cations and measured anions is known as the anion gap . Following is the equation used to measure the anion gap: Serum anion gap = serum sodium - (serum chloride + bicarbonate) Increased concentration of organic acids like lactate, ketones (such as beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate), oxalic acid, formic acid, or glycolic acid , without a corresponding rise in Cl - , is a sign of a high anion gap. Normal anion gap: Cl - compensates for the major loss of HCO3 - In this patient, increased organic acids i.e., ketones in the blood causing high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Factors that affect how severe metabolic acidosis is and how much the anion gap widens: The duration and rate of synthesis of ketoacids The pace at which the ketoacids are metabolized The rate of urine's elimination of ketoacid anions The volume of the ketoacid anions’ dispersion Renal net acid excretion rate Incorrect Options: Option B- Increased lactate: Increased lactate is one of the causes of high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Lactic acidosis is usually seen in the case of poor perfusion leading to anaerobic metabolism e.g limb ischemia, thromboembolism, and mesenteric ischemia. This patient, a known type 1 diabetic is having typical symptoms of diabetic ketoacidosis. Option C- Vomiting: Vomiting due to gastroenteritis/gastric outlet obstruction leads to the loss of a significant amount of HCl from the stomach. This leads to disproportionately high HCO3 ions in the blood causing metabolic alkalosis. This patient’s vomiting is secondary to elevated ketones in the blood leading to frequent gastric irritation. Option D- Increased respiratory rate: Increased respiratory rate leads to the washing out of CO 2 from the blood. Loss of carbon dioxide leads to respiratory alkalosis. This patient’s pH is less than 7.35 and has low bicarbonate ion concentration indicating metabolic acidosis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 24-year-old male presents with a history of headaches. Physical exam is notable for a blood pressure of 192/110 mmHg in the right arm, heart rate of 70 beats/min, normal JVP and carotid upstrokes, an apical S4, no abdominal bruits, and reduced femoral pulses in both lower extremities. Physical exam is notable for a blood pressure of 192/110 mmHg in the right arm, heart rate of 70 beats/min, normal JVP and carotid upstrokes, an apical S4, no abdominal bruits, and reduced femoral pulses in both lower extremities. This patient is most likely to demonstrate which of the following on echocardiography?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Bicuspid aortic valve: This patient has aortic coarctation and is presenting with marked hypertension proximal to the obstructive lesion. The narrowing most commonly occurs distal to the left subclavian, explaining the diminished lower extremity pulses. The incidence of a bicuspid aortic valve in patients with coarctation of the aorta is also elevated. However, the incidence of aortic coarctation in patients with a bicuspid aortic valve is <5%. Ec hocardiography, MRI or CT of the thorax with contrast, or cardiac catheterization can be diagnostic. Pulse wave Doppler of the abdominal aorta shows the classic sawtooth flow pattern with an elevated peak systolic velocity and diastolic run-off secondary to collateral circulation. Incorrect Options: Option B - Mitral stenosis: Mitral stenosis primarily affects the left atrium and left ventricle. It leads to elevated pressure in the left atrium and pulmonary circulation, which could manifest with symptoms like dyspnea, fatigue, and atrial fibrillation. While mitral stenosis could potentially cause some degree of systemic hypertension, it is less likely to be the primary cause of the clinical findings described in this patient. Option C - Preexcitation syndrome: Preexcitation syndromes like Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome involve an accessory pathway that can lead to early ventricular depolarization and characteristic findings on the electrocardiogram (EKG). While these syndromes might present with palpitations or tachyarrhythmias, they are not directly associated with the clinical signs of hypertension, diminished femoral pulses, and aortic obstruction seen in this patient. Option D - Left bundle branch block: Left bundle branch block (LBBB) is an electrical conduction abnormality that affects the ventricular activation sequence. It can be seen on an EKG and may have various underlying causes, including structural heart disease. However, LBBB is not directly linked to the specific clinical presentation of hypertension and reduced femoral pulses associated with aortic coarctation and a possible bicuspid aortic valve. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 60-year-old female with diet-controlled diabetes mellitus presents with nausea, weight loss, and abdominal distention. She had an IUD placed for 15 years that was removed 1 year ago. An earlier CT of her abdomen and pelvis revealed a large solid/cystic pelvic mass and enlarged lymph nodes. She was conservatively managed with intravenous fluids and analgesics and sent home with an outpatient surgical appointment. Today, she returns to the ER with abdominal pain and poor oral intake. Vitals are as follows: BP 121/70, T 98.8°F, HR 107, and RR 18. Abdominal exam reveals a palpable firm mass that is diffusely tender, faint bowel sounds, and guarding but no rebound tenderness. Lungs are clear to auscultation, and heart sounds are normal but tachycardic. Abdominal X-ray shows possible ileus with no obstruction. Repeat CT of the patient's abdomen and pelvis shows a pelvic mass, small bowel distention suggesting partial small bowel obstruction, and worsening hydronephrosis. Exploratory laparotomy followed by a total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral oophorectomy reveal a complex ovarian cyst with multiple abscesses. Pelvic fluid culture microscopy shows non-acid-fast, gram-positive bacilli that are not viable in culture and negative for malignant cells. Surgical pathology is consistent with a tubo-ovarian abscess with gram-positive bacilli. Which organism is the likely cause of this patient's presentation?

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Actinomyces israelii: This patient has an Actinomyces tubo-ovarian abscess. Actinomycosis is a rare and insidious disease; the most common etiologic organism is the filamentous anaerobic gram-positive bacterium Actinomyces israelii. There are 3 main clinical forms of this disease: cervicofacial (50-65%), thoracic (15%), and abdominopelvic (20%). Risk factors for abdominal and pelvic actinomycosis are perforated viscus, tubo-ovarian abscess, abdominal surgery, and intrauterine contraceptive devices. Abdominal actinomycosis can be easily confused with tuberculosis, Crohn's disease, and malignancy. Often, the diagnosis is made postoperatively since most patients undergo exploratory laparotomy for suspected malignancy. Definitive diagnosis is made upon histological identification of actinomycotic sulfur granules and/or culture of Actinomyces. The other organisms listed are gram-positive cocci. questions.stem: A 23-year-old female @ 35 weeks arrives via ambulance stating, "I think my water just broke." She denies contractions. Which of the following should be avoided when performing your exam?
questions.stemHtml: A 23-year-old female @ 35 weeks arrives via ambulance stating, "I think my water just broke." She denies contractions. Which of the following should be avoided when performing your exam?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Digital exam of the cervix: Examination of women with potential premature rupture of membranes should be performed under sterile conditions to prevent ascending infection. Direct digital examination of the cervix should be avoided. Identification of amniotic fluid using nitrazine paper or ferning technique is recommended. Visualization of the cervix for prolapsed cord or abnormal fetal presentation should be done during uterine evaluation for effacement and dilation. Cultures for group B strep, chlamydia, and gonorrhea should be obtained Incorrect Options: Option A - Nitrazine test: Nitrazine test indicates if there is true amniotic fluid present or if there is just increased cervical discharge. This would be an indicated test. Option C - Visualization of cervix: Visulization of the cervix is preferred to determine if there is any dilation. Since it is unknown if the amniotic sac has ruptured yet, digital exam of the cervix should be avoided. Option D - Chlamydia cultures: Chlamydia cultures along with GBS and gonorrhoea should be obtained @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl falls while holding hands with an adult. Afterward, she holds her arm in a pronated position and refuses to use her hand or elbow. She is taken to the emergency department, where the injury is reduced manually. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 6-year-old girl falls while holding hands with an adult. Afterward, she holds her arm in a pronated position and refuses to use her hand or elbow. She is taken to the emergency department, where the injury is reduced manually. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.text: Apophyseal avulsion fracture of the medial humeral epicondyle

questions.solution: Correct Option C- Subluxation of the radial head: This is the classic presentation of nursemaid's elbow (subluxation of the radial head), which results when the annular ligament that passes around the elbow partially slips off the radial head with traction across the elbow. The subluxation is usually caused by traction from a pull on the extended elbow, commonly when a child is lifted by the hand or falls while holding hands with an adult. Clinically, the hand is held in a pronated position and the child will refuse to use the hand or move the elbow. The elbow can usually be reduced by apply pressure to the radial head and moving the hand into the supinated position. Nursemaid's elbow is usually a clinical diagnosis and x-rays are not necessary unless the injury cannot be reduced or if there is swelling and bruising that prompt concern for fracture. After reduction, the child will use the arm normally. Incorrect Options: Options A & B- (Osteochondritis dissecans of the capitellum & Apophyseal avulsion fracture of the medial humeral epicondyle): Osteochondritis dissecans of the capitellum and apophyseal avulsion fracture of the medial humeral epicondyle are associated with Little Leaguer's Elbow, a group of repetitive overuse injuries commonly seen in adolescent throwing athletes. Option D-Scaphoid fracture: Scaphoid fracture is the most common fracture of the carpal bones in children, which would not manifest in this way. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Hypocalcemia from citrate : Citrate is used as an anticoagulant in blood products, including packed red blood cells (pRBCs). When blood products containing citrate are transfused, citrate binds to calcium ions in the patient's bloodstream, forming complexes that are then metabolized in the liver. In patients with liver dysfunction, the metabolism of citrate can be impaired, leading to a buildup of citrate and a subsequent decrease in ionized calcium levels. This can result in hypocalcemia, which can have various clinical manifestations, including neurological symptoms such as seizures. In this case, the patient's history of alcoholic cirrhosis and the large volume of blood products transfused could contribute to impaired citrate metabolism and subsequent hypocalcemia. Incorrect Options: Option B - Hypercalcemia from excess glycerol: Glycerol is not commonly used in blood products and is not associated with causing hypercalcemia. Excess 2,3-BPG would not cause hypercalcemia. Option D - Hypocalcemia from EDTA: EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid) is another anticoagulant used in blood products. questions.answerText: Asthma is characterized by airway obstruction that is partially or completely reversible with treatment.
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Asthma is characterized by airway obstruction that is partially or completely reversible with treatment: Asthma is a reversible condition that affects the airways of the lungs. During an asthma attack or exacerbation, the airways become inflamed, narrowed, and produce excessive mucus, leading to symptoms such as coughing, wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. In most cases, the airway obstruction in asthma is reversible , either spontaneously or with appropriate treatment. The degree of reversibility can vary from person to person and can depend on factors such as the severity and duration of the asthma attack, the individual's age and overall health, and the effectiveness of the treatment. However, in some cases, repeated and severe asthma attacks can lead to irreversible lung damage and a decline in lung function, known as airway remodelling. Airway remodelling is characterized by structural changes in the airways, such as increased smooth muscle and collagen deposition, which can lead to persistent airflow limitation and reduced response to bronchodilators. This irreversible lung damage is more likely to occur in individuals with severe and uncontrolled asthma, particularly those who smoke or have other risk factors such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).. Incorrect Options: Option B - Asthma is caused by irreversible damage to the airways, leading to permanent airway obstruction: Asthma is a reversible condition that can be managed with appropriate treatment. Irreversible damage to the airways can occur in other obstructive lung diseases like chronic bronchitis or emphysema. Option C - Asthma is caused by chronic bronchitis, leading to narrowing of the airways: Asthma and chronic bronchitis are two distinct diseases with different underlying pathophysiology. Chronic bronchitis is characterized by chronic inflammation and mucus production in the bronchi, leading to airway obstruction and impaired gas exchange. Option D - Asthma is caused by emphysema, leading to decreased lung elasticity: Asthma and emphysema are two distinct diseases with different underlying pathophysiology. Emphysema is a type of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) characterized by destruction of the alveolar walls, leading to loss of lung elasticity and impaired gas exchange. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following cellular processes is a key contributor to the aging process by increasing the chances of mutations and replicative senescence?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following cellular processes is a key contributor to the aging process by increasing the chances of mutations and replicative senescence?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Telomere shortening: Telomeres are protective caps at the ends of chromosomes, and they shorten with each cell division. When telomeres become critically short, cells can no longer divide, leading to replicative senescence. Additionally, as telomeres shorten, there is an increased risk of DNA mutations, which are associated with the aging process. Incorrect Options: Option A - Oxidative stress: While oxidative stress is a contributing factor to aging, it primarily involves the accumulation of damage from reactive oxygen species. Option B - Impaired autophagy: Impaired autophagy is a cellular process in which cells remove unnecessary components, but it is not a primary contributor to telomere shortening or replicative senescence. Option D - Proteostasis dysfunction: Proteostasis dysfunction involves the accumulation of harmful proteins due to impaired clearance by proteases. While it is a cellular process associated with aging, it is not directly linked to telomere shortening or replicative senescence. @Neet_pg_bot

options.label: B

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman presents to the emergency room due to increasing shortness of breath for one day. She states it has been worsening over months, and she now struggles to perform daily tasks like cleaning and cooking. She has no chest pain during these episodes but has to sit to catch her breath. She has a history of hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and myocardial infarction. On examination, she has +2 lower limb oedema, raised JVP, and bilateral lung crackles. The patient is given IV Nitroglycerin, and his dyspnea improves. Which of the following is the best explanation for this patient’s improvement in symptoms?

She has a history of hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and myocardial infarction. On examination, she has +2 lower limb oedema, raised JVP, and bilateral lung crackles. The patient is given IV Nitroglycerin, and his dyspnea improves. Which of the following is the best explanation for this patient’s improvement in symptoms?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Preload reduction: The patient in the scenario is presenting with symptoms and signs of heart failure, including dyspnea, lower limb edema, raised JVP, and bilateral lung crackles. IV nitroglycerin was given, which improved the patient's dyspnea. Nitroglycerin is a potent vasodilator that acts by relaxing the smooth muscle in the veins and arterioles. This leads to a reduction in preload, which is the volume of blood in the ventricles at the end of diastole. By reducing preload, nitroglycerin reduces the amount of blood that the heart has to pump with each beat, which can improve symptoms of heart failure like dyspnea and oedema. Coronary artery vasodilation, decreased adrenergic tone, and decreased platelet aggregation are all effects of nitroglycerin, but they are not the primary mechanism by which it improves heart failure symptoms. Incorrect Options: Option A- Coronary artery vasodilation: Coronary artery vasodilation is a mechanism of action by which Nitroglycerin can act and reduce chest pain. However, ischemic myocardium tends to already be maximally vasodilated; thus, the major mechanism in which chest pain is reduced with Nitroglycerin is via preload reduction and subsequent decreased cardiac stretch and contractility (the Frank-Starling principle). Option B- Decreased adrenergic tone: Decreased adrenergic tone describes a beta-blocker such as propranolol. Beta-blockers reduce adrenergic tone in the heart and cardiac oxygen demand, thus reducing mortality. Option D- Decreased platelet aggregation: Decreased platelet aggregation describes the mechanism of action of aspirin. Aspirin is the best initial step in the management of a patient experiencing acute coronary syndrome as it reduces mortality and is easy and fast to administer. @Neet_pg_bot

This particular case belongs to group II which includes pulmonary hypertension secondary to heart failure (systolic or diastolic) and valvular diseases. questions.stem: A 19-year-old male presents to the ER after a stab wound posterior to the medial epicondyle of the humerus. The sensory nerve supply to the area of injury is provided by which of the following nerves?
questions.stemHtml: A 19-year-old male presents to the ER after a stab wound posterior to the medial epicondyle of the humerus. The sensory nerve supply to the area of injury is provided by which of the following nerves?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- T1: Examination of the upper extremity is critical in patients with traumatic injuries to determine underlying pathology. Understanding the upper extremity dermatomes helps facilitate accurate diagnosis, management, and response to therapy. The medial aspect of the elbow, including the posterior median epicondyle and skin overlying the medial epicondyle, is innervated by the T1 (or first thoracic) dermatome. Imaging may be needed to rule out underlying fracture. Isolated medial epicondyle fractures usually occur in children and adolescents and often result from posterior elbow dislocations, repeated stress (e.g., throwing a baseball), or a direct blow. Examination findings of blunt trauma affecting this dermatome include pain and swelling over the medial epicondyle and painful elbow flexion or forearm supination. Nondisplaced or minimally displaced medial epicondyle fractures are managed nonoperatively with early range of motion. Complications include ulnar nerve palsy and avascular necrosis. Incorrect Options: Option A- C6: Sensation of the thumb assesses the C6 dermatome. Sensation of the dorsal surface of the proximal phalanx of the thumb grossly assesses the sensory function of the radial nerve. Option B- C7: Sensation of the tip of the third (or long) finger assesses the C7 dermatome. This also grossly assesses the sensory function of the median nerve. Option C- C8: Sensation of the tip of the fifth (or little) finger assesses the C8 dermatome. This also grossly assesses the sensory function of the ulnar nerve. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A- Hypocalcemia: The patient is experiencing hypocalcemia secondary to chronic renal failure. The normal range of serum calcium is 8.5-10.5 mg/dL. Hypocalcemia can cause a range of symptoms, including muscle weakness, tingling or numbness in the fingers and toes, and difficulty breathing. Causes of hypocalcemia can include hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, chronic renal failure, and malabsorption syndromes. Carpal Spasm (abnormal flexion of the wrist) secondary to brachial artery occlusion using a BP cuff is called Trousseau Sign which manifests in hypocalcemia. Chevostek Sign is the twitching of facial muscles when areas supplied by facial nerves are tapped. It also manifests in hypocalcemia Incorrect Options: Option B- Hypercalcemia: It refers to high serum calcium levels and can be caused by hyperparathyroidism, malignancy, or excess vitamin D intake. It presents with renal stones, constipation, fatigue, irritability and forgetfulness. Option C- Hypomagnesemia: It refers to low serum magnesium levels and can cause symptoms similar to hypocalcemia, including muscle weakness and tingling sensations. However, hypomagnesemia typically does not cause difficulty breathing. Severe hypomagnesemia can cause dysfunction of Calcium sensing receptors leading to low PTH and subsequent hypocalcemia but it is least likely the cause of patients symptoms in this case Option D- Hypophosphatemia: It refers to low serum phosphorus levels and can be caused by Vitamin D resistance or deficient osteomalacia, diuretics, bronchodilators and Primary hyperparathyroidism. Symptomatic hypophosphatemia develops when serum phosphate falls below 1.0 mg/dL. It presents as dysarthria, respiratory failure, muscle weakness and paraesthesias. In renal failure patients, there is usually hyperphosphatemia despite PTH elevation ( secondary Hyperparathyroidism ) due to failure of phosphate of excretion. @Neet_pg_bot

This constellation of findings is most consistent with acute pericarditis. The pericardium is a double-layered sac that surrounds the heart and contains a small amount of fluid that lubricates the heart during its contractions. Acute pericarditis is an inflammatory condition of the pericardium that can cause severe chest pain , often radiating to the left arm, and ECG changes that mimic ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). Echocardiography may reveal an echo-free space around the heart, indicating the presence of pericardial effusion. Incorrect Options: Option B- Myocardial infarction: Although ST-segment elevation on ECG is a hallmark finding of myocardial infarction (MI), the presence of an echo-free space around the heart on echocardiography suggests pericarditis rather than MI. Echocardiography is not typically used to diagnose aortic dissection . Option D- Pulmonary embolism: Pulmonary embolism can cause chest pain, but it is typically associated with other symptoms such as shortness of breath and tachycardia . ECG changes and an echo-free space around the heart are not characteristic findings of pulmonary embolism. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A woman at 34 weeks of gestation presents to the emergency department with fever, headache, diarrhea, and malaise. Her temperature on admission is 102°F (38.9°C). Shortly thereafter, the amniotic membranes rupture and the fluid is dark, cloudy, and green-tinged. The newborn is in severe respiratory distress at delivery, but has no congenital malformations. Small pustules are scattered over the trunk. Microscopic examination of the amniotic fluid reveals Gram-positive rods. History reveals that the mother lives on a farm and drinks unpasteurized milk. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of illness in the mother and newborn?
questions.stemHtml: A woman at 34 weeks of gestation presents to the emergency department with fever, headache, diarrhea, and malaise. Her temperature on admission is 102°F (38.9°C). Shortly thereafter, the amniotic membranes rupture and the fluid is dark, cloudy, and green-tinged. The newborn is in severe respiratory distress at delivery, but has no congenital malformations. Small pustules are scattered over the trunk. Microscopic examination of the amniotic fluid reveals Gram-positive rods. History reveals that the mother lives on a farm and drinks unpasteurized milk. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of illness in the mother and newborn?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Listeria monocytogenes: Listeria monocytogenes is an uncommon cause of prenatal infection, but fetal effects can be severe. Mothers are typically infected by the ingestion of contaminated foods . Most commonly, these are cured meats, unpasteurized dairy products (e.g., milk, soft cheeses), melons, or undercooked foods. Listeria has a predilection for placenta, liver, spleen, and the CNS. Infection in the 3rd trimester can lead to preterm delivery, and the amniotic fluid is often stained with meconium. Neonatal infection with Listeria occurs in early and late forms. Early-onset, or congenital, infection manifests in the first day of life, and usually results from placental infection. Ascending infection from the vagina is also thought to be possible. Affected newborns often have sepsis and may be in respiratory distress from pneumonia. Small pustular lesions, called granulomatosis infantisepticum , may be seen. The mortality rate from early Listeria sepsis is substantial, at 20-60%. Late-onset infection occurs at a few weeks of age, often presenting as meningitis. This pattern of early and late presentation is similar to that seen with Group B Streptococcus, a common cause of neonatal sepsis. Laboratory studies are not specific for Listeria, and diagnosis relies on culture and microscopic examination of infected material. The organisms are classically described as Gram-positive rods, which may be seen intracellularly . However, Listeria may be Gram-variable and can appear pleomorphic, making differentiation from other bacteria difficult. Treatment of Listeria infection is with intravenous antibiotics . All neonatal L. monocytogenes infections are considered sensitive to ampicillin (and penicillin), and this is the drug of choice. The addition of gentamicin may have synergistic effects. Listeria is now a reportable disease, and the identification of a case may lead to the discovery of an outbreak with public health implications. Spread within a nursery is also possible, so care must be taken to prevent cross-contamination in the neonatal unit Incorrect Options: Option A - E.coli: The bacteria in the amniotic fluid are Gram-positive rods, whereas E. coli are Gram-negative rods. Option B - Streptococcus pneumoniae: Streptococcus pneumoniae are Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci. They are a very uncommon cause of neonatal sepsis and are not consistent with the presentation in this case. Option C - Toxoplasma gondii: Toxoplasma gondii is a parasite capable of causing a wide range of severe fetal and long-term effects. However, the presentation is not typically one of overt maternal illness preceding a preterm delivery. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Cardiac conduction defects, pigmentary retinopathy, and disease onset before age 20 : While there is considerable overlap in the features of mitochondrial cytopathies that present with CPEO, distinct differences in the hallmark features exist. It occasionally presents with CPEO. questions.stem: A 60-year-old male presents for evaluation of hematochezia for 3 months. His colonoscopy revealed a 6 cm adenocarcinoma in the cecum, with a 4 mm adenoma near the splenic flexure. The adenoma is removed completely. His father also had 4 small colorectal adenomas on colonoscopy when he was 58 years old, but there is otherwise no family history of colorectal cancer or polyps. Immunohistochemistry and microsatellite instability testing reveal high tumor MSI with loss of MSH2 and 6. Expression of MLH1 and PMS2 is normal, and there are no detectable germline mutations in MSH2 or MSH6. What is the next step in the management of this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old male presents for evaluation of hematochezia for 3 months. His colonoscopy revealed a 6 cm adenocarcinoma in the cecum, with a 4 mm adenoma near the splenic flexure. The adenoma is removed completely. His father also had 4 small colorectal adenomas on colonoscopy when he was 58 years old, but there is otherwise no family history of colorectal cancer or polyps. Immunohistochemistry and microsatellite instability testing reveal high tumor MSI with loss of MSH2 and 6. Expression of MLH1 and PMS2 is normal, and there are no detectable germline mutations in MSH2 or MSH6. What is the next step in the management of this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: This is sporadic colorectal cancer, and no further evaluation is indicated

options.label: B
options.text: Genetic testing is indicated for an EPCAM mutation

options.label: C
options.text: BRAF testing is indicated for MLH1 hypermethylation

options.label: D
options.text: Full genetic sequencing for PMS2 is indicated

questions.answerText: Genetic testing is indicated for an EPCAM mutation
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Genetic testing is indicated for an EPCAM mutation: This patient may have Lynch syndrome due to an EPCAM mutation. Lynch syndrome refers to hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer and is associated with a 25-75% lifetime risk of colorectal cancer. With familial adenomatous polyposis, it is the most common cause of familial colorectal cancer, yet both conditions account for only about 5% of CRC. It is characterized by a genetic or de novo disease-causing defect in a mismatch repair (MMR) gene. This results in microsatellite instability (MSI) that can be detected by polymerase chain reaction. The absence of microsatellite instability with the intact expression of all 4 MMR proteins eliminates Lynch syndrome as a diagnosis. The absence of protein expression of an MMR protein, MLH1 and PMS2, PMS2 alone, or MLH1 alone is sometimes associated with sporadic cancers as well as with inherited CRC. Loss of expression of MSH2, MSH2 with MSH6, or MSH 6 alone are all specific for a germline defect as the cause of CRC. This should prompt referral for genetic testing. If genetic testing does not show a mutation in MSH2, then EPCAM genetic testing should be the next step. Although EPCAM is not a mismatch repair protein, it may affect MSH2 expression. There have been reports of EPCAM deletions in patients with Lynch syndrome. Incorrect Options: Options A - This is sporadic colorectal cancer, and no further evaluation is indicated: False, Loss of MSH2 and MSH6 suggests Lynch syndrome. Options C - BRAF testing is indicated for MLH1 hypermethylation: False, Methylation of the MLH1 promoter without a BRAF mutation should prompt consideration of a genetic defect. If MLH1 and PMS2, PMS2 alone, or MLH1 alone are not expressed, analysis of BRAF mutation or methylation of the MLH1 promoter is indicated. A BRAF mutation suggests sporadic disease, so further genetic testing is not required. Options D - Full genetic sequencing for PMS2 is indicated: False, Genetic testing for PMS2 is not indicated. Defects in PMS2 alone are rarely the cause of Lynch syndrome, and PMS2 expression is normal. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Blood Hemodialysis: The patient with asterixis, e.g., a bilateral nonrhythmic alternate flexion and extension movements at rest called flapping tremors, confusion, and abnormal renal functional tests, has most likely the diagnosis of uremic encephalopathy. questions.stemHtml: A 46-year-old man presents with a history of fatigue, hypertension, and swelling in his feet and ankles for six months. On physical examination, his blood pressure is 150/90 mmHg, and he has 2+ pitting oedema in his lower extremities. Urinalysis shows proteinuria (3+), hematuria, and red blood cell casts. A renal biopsy reveals thickening of the capillary basement membrane, mesangial proliferation, and subendothelial deposits. The patient is diagnosed with membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN). Which of the following best describes the pathophysiology of MPGN?

options.label: A
options.text: Circulating immune complexes deposit in the glomerular basement membrane and activate complement, leading to inflammation and glomerular injury

options.label: B
options.text: Anti-GBM antibodies bind to the glomerular basement membrane, leading to the immune complex formation and complement activation

options.label: C
options.text: Podocyte injury leads to the detachment of podocytes from the glomerular basement membrane, resulting in proteinuria and glomerulosclerosis

options.label: D
options.text: Mesangial cell proliferation leads to the thickening of the glomerular basement membrane and narrowing of the capillary lumen, resulting in decreased glomerular filtration rate

questions.answerText: Circulating immune complexes deposit in the glomerular basement membrane and activate complement, leading to inflammation and glomerular injury
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Circulating immune complexes deposit in the glomerular basement membrane and activate complement, leading to inflammation and glomerular injury MPGN is characterized by immune complex deposition in the glomerular basement membrane and mesangium, leading to activation of the complement system and inflammation. The classical pathway of complement activation is activated, forming a membrane attack complex and subsequent glomerular injury. questions.solution: Correct Option C- Improved bone mineral density: Kidney transplantation is a life-saving treatment for end-stage renal disease (ESRD) patients. In addition to improving patient survival, kidney transplantation significantly benefits the patient's quality of life. One such benefit is an improvement in bone mineral density. ESRD patients are at increased risk of developing bone mineral disorders due to several factors, including impaired vitamin D metabolism, secondary hyperparathyroidism, and metabolic acidosis. Transplantation can improve these metabolic abnormalities and lead to an improvement in bone mineral density. Incorrect Options: Option A- Increased risk of hypertension: Although hypertension is a common complication of kidney transplantation, it is not a long-term outcome associated with kidney transplantation. Hypertension can occur due to immunosuppressive medications and can also be related to pre-existing cardiovascular disease. Option B- Increased risk of diabetes mellitus: While diabetes mellitus is a common cause of ESRD and may require kidney transplantation, transplantation itself does not increase the risk of diabetes mellitus. Immunosuppressive medications may increase the risk of glucose intolerance and insulin resistance, but this is usually reversible with dose adjustment or discontinuation of the medication. Option D- Increased risk of malignancy: Immunosuppressive medications used after kidney transplantation increase the risk of malignancy, but this is not a long-term outcome. Instead, it is a potential complication of the treatment . Patients receiving immunosuppressive medications are at increased risk of skin cancers, lymphomas, and other malignancies. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A- Induction chemo + TKI + IT chemo: In this scenario, the patient has been diagnosed with Ph+ ALL in blast crisis, and she also has central nervous system (CNS) involvement. Given her history of chronic phase CML with the p210 BCR-ABL fusion gene, it's crucial to address both the systemic disease and the CNS involvement. Induction chemotherapy: Induction chemotherapy is essential for rapidly reducing the high blast count in the peripheral blood and bone marrow. This aims to achieve remission in the systemic disease. Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitor (TKI): TKIs like imatinib, dasatinib, or ponatinib are critical in treating Ph+ ALL with a history of CML. These drugs target the BCR-ABL fusion protein, which drives the disease. TKIs are essential for systemic control of the disease. Intrathecal (IT) chemotherapy: CNS involvement in Ph+ ALL is a significant concern because TKIs have limited penetration of the blood-brain barrier. Intrathecal chemotherapy, which involves the direct injection of chemotherapy drugs into the cerebrospinal fluid, is needed to target and treat leukemia cells in the CNS. Therefore, a combination of induction chemotherapy, a TKI to target systemic disease, and IT chemotherapy to address CNS involvement is the most comprehensive and effective approach for this patient. questions.stemHtml: A 36-year-old homosexual man who has just returned from an extended trip to Africa presents to his primary care physician with anorectal spasms, pain, bloody discharge, and peri-anal sores. Which test will provide the greatest sensitivity on a specimen collected from the anal sores?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Rapid, multiplex, real-time PCR Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2 and L3, which are distinct from those that cause the more common form of Chlamydial disease (serovars D-K). The LGV strains are most often found in Africa, Southeastern Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean. Sporadic cases of LGV have occurred in North America, although these are thought to have been imported. During the first phase of the infection, patients present with an ulcerative disease. These ulcers are usually small and of short duration. After the resolution of the ulcers, there are two main presentations of this disease: the classical inguinal syndrome as well as the anorectal syndrome. In the inguinal syndrome, the bacteria spread via the lymphatic system to cause inguinal lymphadenopathy with the formation of buboes. If the disease is left untreated, the surrounding tissue structures can be destroyed, leading to fistulas and damage to the lymphatic system. In severe cases, it may result in elephantiasis. Typical anorectal symptoms include spasms, perianal sores, bloody discharge, pain, and constipation (as in this case). Multiplex real-time PCR is specific for the detection of LGV associated L-serovars and enables the differentiation of L1, L2, and L3 for epidemiologic studies. Incorrect Options: Option B - Culture: Culture is another diagnostic option, but this is not serovar specific. Option C - Serology with complement fixation: Serology with complement fixation can support the diagnosis of LGV (complement fixation titers >1:64), but these methods are not standardized. Hence, there is limited information about how well they perform or how to interpret the results. Option D - Genetic probe method: Genetic probe methods may be accurate but are not as sensitive as nucleic acid amplification methods. @Neet_pg_bot

Intervention is required to prevent the progression to carcinoma. questions.solution: Correct Option D- ACE inhibitor-induced cough: The patient's symptoms of dry cough, dyspnea, and wheezing suggest a respiratory complication. ACE inhibitors are commonly used in the treatment of heart failure because they improve left ventricular function, decrease afterload, and reduce blood pressure. However, one of the most common side effects of ACE inhibitors is a dry cough. This cough is due to the accumulation of bradykinin, a potent vasodilator, in the lungs. Bradykinin stimulates sensory nerves in the lungs, causing coughing. The cough associated with ACE inhibitors is typically dry, persistent, and nonproductive. It may occur anytime during treatment, but is more common in the first few weeks. The cough usually resolves within days to weeks after discontinuation of the drug. Pain is sharp, limited to the anterior chest, worsens with recumbent position, and improves with sitting upright. On examination, blood pressure is 90/60mmHg and heart rate 100/min. His JVP is raised, and precordial auscultation reveals a pericardial friction rub with muffled heart sounds. ECG shows low amplitude complexes and electrical alternans. He is subsequently diagnosed with acute pericarditis complicated with massive pericardial effusion. What is the normal physiologic amount of pericardial fluid in the pericardial sac?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Up to 50 ml: A healthy pericardium contains up to 50 ml of clear serous fluid. The pericardium comprises two layers: inner visceral and outer parietal pericardium. The visceral pericardium adheres to the epicardium and comprises collagen, elastin fiber and a layer of mesothelial cells. The parietal layers surround the heat and are fibrous and acellular. The pericardial sac or space is formed between the visceral and parietal pericardium and physiologically contains up to 50 ml of serous fluid. The pericardial fluid is a cushion between two layers of the pericardium, thereby reducing friction during the cardiac cycle. The normal composition of pericardial fluid is almost the same as plasma ultrafiltrate , with lymphocytes being the predominant cell type. The elasticity of the pericardium is limited, and only a small amount of acutely collected pericardial fluid can lead to cardiac tamponade , where excessive pericardial fluid compresses heart chambers, especially the thinner right heart. This impairs the diastolic ventricular filling and venous congestion, reducing stroke volume and hypotension. Incorrect Options: Option A - Up to 200 ml: This is not the normal amount of pericardial fluid in healthy individuals. This amount of pericardial fluid is enough to result in a radiologically evident pericardial effusion. Enlargement of the cardiac silhouette occurs when the pericardium has 200ml or more fluid in its cavity. Option C - Up to 250 ml: This is not the normal amount of pericardial fluid in healthy individuals. This amount of fluid, when collected chronically, is enough to make the patient highly symptomatic with shortness of breath and engorged neck veins. The presence of chronically collected 250 ml of pericardial fluid indicates imminent cardiac tamponade. Option D - Up to 300ml: This is not the normal amount of pericardial fluid in healthy individuals. A chronically collected 300 ml or more pericardial fluid causes pericardial tamponade. That much amount of pericardial fluid requires emergent therapeutic pericardiocentesis. @Neet_pg_bot
